questionStem: A 6-year-old girl in remission of acute lymphoblastic leukemia has had pain in her right shoulder for 2 days. She is receiving maintenance chemotherapy and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly P. carini1) pneumonia . She has a 4 x 1-cm, erythematous patch beneath the right scapula with six to eight superimposed , small, clear fluid-filled vesicles . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this rash?
correctExplanation: This patient's immunocompromise and vesicular eruption is consistent with reactivation of varicella zoster virus in the form of herpes zoster infection. Varicella zoster virus infection (VZV), also known as human herpesvirus-3 (HHV-3), is transmitted via respiratory secretions and direct contact with infected skin lesions. It causes two diseases: varicella and herpes zoster. Varicella causes chickenpox in immunocompetent children which is characterized by a pruritic, asynchronous rash with fluid-filled vesicles that crust. The vesicles heal as crusted papules and lesions are in various stages of healing. Varicella can cause encephalitis and pneumonia in immunosuppressed patients, such as an individual being treated with chemotherapy. Herpes zoster is caused by the recurrence of VZV after it has been reactivated from its dormancy in the dorsal root ganglion of a spinal nerve. It commonly presents as a unilateral, dermatomal erythematous patch with overlying clear to yellow, grouped vesicles. It can be associated with neuropathic pain which can precede and outlast the rash. However, post-herpetic neuralgia is more common in elderly patients than pediatric patients. The thoracic spinal nerves and trigeminal nerve are particularly common distributions of reactivation. Treatment for herpetic infections, including herpes zoster infections, involves medications that inhibit viral DNA polymerase, classically by guanosine analogs such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Coxsackievirus (Choice A) is an enterovirus which causes hand, foot, and mouth disease. This presents with painful oval-shaped vesicles on the palms, soles, and oral mucosa. Coxsackievirus is also the cause of herpangina, an infection of the posterior pharynx which usually involves the tonsils, soft palate, and uvula. Examination of these sites shows erythema caused by hyperemia and yellow to gray papulovesicular lesions. Herpes simplex virus (Choice B) is typically transmitted through contact with infected skin or mucosal surfaces, and can present with a variety of symptoms, including genital herpes, herpes labialis, herpetic whitlow, encephalitis, esophagitis, and keratoconjunctivitis. This patient's dermatomal distribution favors herpes zoster over a cutaneous herpes simplex virus infection. Leukemic relapse (Choice D) can present with a rash in the form of leukemia cutis. Leukemia cutis is caused by infiltration of the epidermis and dermis with leukemic cells. It has a range of presentations, but firm papules or subcutaneous nodules, not vesicles, are most common. Toxic drug reaction (Choice E), or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), is a severe cutaneous drug reaction which has a high mortality rate. It is characterized by large areas of dusky erythema with desquamation of the epidermis. It is often complicated by infection of the denuded areas of skin. The confinement of small vesicles to a single dermatome without spreading would be highly uncharacteristic of TEN. Educational Objective: Herpes zoster is caused by reactivation of dormant varicella zoster virus infection in the dorsal root ganglion of a spinal nerve. It most commonly presents with grouped clear to yellow vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution.

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of intermittent right knee pain for 2 months . The pain typically occurs in the morning and after naps. She has not had fever, rash, or symptoms in any other joint. She plays soccer twice weekly but has not had any injuries . Her parents recall that she had a sore throat for 2 days prior to the onset of her knee pain. There is no family history of osteoarthritis . She is at the 25th percentile for height, 70th percentile for weight , and above the 97th percentile for BMI. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows slight bowing of the lower extremities . The right knee is larger than the left knee. There is tenderness of the right knee to palpation . Range of motion of the right knee is decreased . Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 45 mm/h. X-rays of the knees show no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.D: Tear of the anterior cruciate ligament

correctExplanation: Juvenile arthritis (juvenile idiopathic arthritis, or JIA) occurs before the age of 16 and is a common rheumatic disease among children. The disease has an autoimmune cause and is characterized by joint pain and inflammation. Patients commonly exhibit extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, lymphadenopathy, and rash. There are a variety of sub-categories of JIA. For example, oligoarticular disease is characterized by the involvement of fewer than five joints (typically large joints such as the knee) and antinuclear antibody (ANA) positivity; polyarticular disease is characterized by involvement of greater than five joints (typically both large and small joints such as the interphalangeal joints), uveitis, and negative ANA titers, and systemic disease (also known as juvenile onset Still disease) is characterized by variable joint involvement, rash, quotidian fever, and serositis. Diagnosis is often difficult and is based on a combination of characteristic clinical findings and suggestive laboratory tests, such as ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated peptide, and inflammatory tests such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate. There is no single, confirmatory laboratory test for JIA. Treatment modalities include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease modifying antirheumatic medications such as methotrexate, and biologic agents.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute rheumatic fever (Choice A) is a late complication of under- or untreated Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) infection characterized by carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea, and migratory polyarthritis. The cause is related to immune cross-reactivity as a result of molecular homology between streptococcal M protein and human cardiac myosin proteins. Septic arthritis (Choice C) is most commonly bacterial and presents with the rapid onset of fever, joint swelling, erythema, pain, tenderness with range of motion, inability to bear weight, and leukocytosis. Arthrocentesis typically shows bacteria on Gram stain, most often Gram-positive organisms, and leukocyte count is greater than or equal to 50,000/mm 3 with a neutrophilic predominance. Tear of the anterior cruciate ligament (Choice D) commonly presents as an acute injury in athletes when attempting rapid changes in direction upon a planted foot. Patients often report an audible pop when the injury is sustained and experience acute onset of pain, joint swelling, and instability. Tibia vara (Choice E) refers to an outward-bowing deformity of the tibia. It commonly occurs in children with vitamin D deficiency (rickets) or Blount disease. It does not typically manifest with joint swelling. Educational Objective: Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (juvenile idiopathic arthritis, or JIA) occurs before the age of 16 and is the most common rheumatic disease among children. It has an autoimmune cause and is characterized by joint pain and inflammation. Patients also commonly exhibit extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, lymphadenopathy, and rash. Diagnosis is made by a combination of characteristic clinical and laboratory findings.

questionStem: A 7-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus has had fever, cough , and rhinorrhea for 1 week and lethargy for 3 days . His pulse is 100/min, respirations are 30/min , and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. He appears lethargic; no other abnormalities are noted. Serum studies show: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the hyperkalemia?
correctExplanation: Na• CI- K+ HC0 3- Glucose Urea nitrogen 120 mEq/L 95 mEq/L 7.5 mEq/L 10 mEq/L 690 mg/dl 23 mg/dl Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) typically occurs in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus as a result of increased insulin requirements during times of physiologic stress (eg, infection) or insulin nonadherence. DKA occurs as a result of the accumulation of serum ketones in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs because of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Patients may present with complaints of fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Vital signs may show tachycardia and tachypnea. Laboratory studies typically show increased glucose and ketone concentrations, metabolic acidosis, and a high anion-gap caused by the accumulation of unmeasured anions in serum. In metabolic acidosis, excess hydrogen ions are transported into the cell in exchange for potassium ions to maintain electroneutrality. Insulin promotes intracellular potassium entry, and in DKA, insulin deficiency contributes to the excess cellular shift of potassium to the extracellular space resulting in hyperkalemia despite decreased concentrations of total body potassium as a result of excess urinary excretion. Treatment is through replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adrenal insufficiency (Choice A) refers to insufficient production of hormones from the adrenal cortex, which include aldosterone and cortisol; sex hormone deficiency may also be present. Primary adrenal insufficiency can present with deficiencies in both aldosterone and cortisol, whereas secondary and tertiary adrenal insufficiency tend to affect cortisol only. Insufficient aldosterone production leads to hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Insufficient cortisol can lead to hypoglycemia, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, and depressed mental status. In this patient, DKA is more likely given his history of type 1 diabetes, metabolic acidosis, and hyperglycemia. Excessive potassium intake (Choice C) would be unlikely to cause hyperkalemia in this patient. Kidney potassium filtration typically regulates serum potassium within a normal range, but this can be impaired in end­ stage kidney disease. In DKA, the kidney excretion of potassium is increased because of osmotic diuresis. Hyperkalemia in this case is as a result of the extracellular shift of potassium and deficient insulin signaling. Hemolysis (Choice D) can result in hyperkalemia because of the release of intracellular potassium into the serum. DKA is unlikely to cause hemolysis. Hemolytic anemia may present with jaundice and increased bilirubin. Respiratory acidosis (Choice E) would be the opposite of what is expected in a patient with DKA. In DKA, metabolic acidosis leads to compensatory respiratory alkalosis. Kussmaul respirations, which are rapid and deep, are a classic physical examination finding. Educational Objective: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) typically occurs in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus as a result of increased insulin requirements during times of physiologic stress (eg, infection) or insulin

questionStem: While being evaluated for a cardiac murmur, a 12-year-old boy is noted to have bilateral gynecomastia . His sexual development is Tanner stage 3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.C: Evaluate his brothers for this finding
choices.D: Privately tell his parents about the finding
choices.E: Reassure him that this is normal

correctExplanation: Gynecomastia refers to an increase in the amount of glandular breast tissue in males, and it is common during puberty. Pubertal gynecomastia is caused by a disruption in the normal balance of androgens and estrogens and is common in boys aged 12 to 14 years old, typically when they have a sexual maturity rating of 3, as in this patient. The increased concentrations of estrogen are caused by the conversion of androstenedione and testosterone to estrone and estradiol. On physical examination, gynecomastia may be tender to palpation. Results of laboratory studies will be within reference ranges in pubertal gynecomastia but could be used to delineate other causes of gynecomastia. These other causes include medications (eg, spironolactone, ketoconazole, antiandrogen therapy), liver cirrhosis, germ cell tumors, hypogonadism, and hyperthyroidism. Physiologic gynecomastia typically self-resolves but medical and surgical options exist for symptomatic patients, such as aromatase inhibitors and liposuction. As this patient has no signs to suggest pathologic gynecomastia, reassurance is appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Measuring serum corticosteroid concentrations (Choice A) may be useful in the evaluation of suspected Cushing syndrome (high concentrations of baseline cortisol) or Addison disease (deficiency of cortisol). Cushing syndrome presents with weight gain, fatigue, truncal obesity, fat redistribution, hirsutism, and abdominal striae, whereas Addison disease presents with hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation, and abdominal pain. Neither present with gynecomastia as a direct result, though truncal obesity may resemble it in Cushing syndrome (or in Cushing disease). Measuring serum gonadotropin concentrations (Choice B) may be useful in the evaluation of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, such as Klinefelter syndrome, which can present with gynecomastia. However, patients with Klinefelter syndrome typically have testicular atrophy, tall stature, and long extremities, which this patient does not exhibit. Evaluating his brother for this finding (Choice C) may be useful if the gynecomastia was because of a hereditary disorder, such as partial androgen insensitivity or aromatase excess. However, this patient is presenting with mild gynecomastia associated with puberty, making physiologic gynecomastia more likely. Privately telling his parents about the finding (Choice D) is inappropriate, as the condition is benign, and the patient should be included in health conversations regarding his body. Educational Objective: Physiologic pubertal gynecomastia is a benign proliferation of glandular breast tissue in boys aged 12 to 14 years, most commonly during at the sexual maturity rating of 3 during puberty.

questionStem: A 4-month-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . She is breast-feeding successfully and has been in good health. She is able to roll from her stomach to her back, and she looks around with curiosity, coos, and orients to voice . Her parents are concerned about a lesion on her left thigh that has become darker since birth. The patient appears well. She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. Examination of the left thigh shows the brown lesion seen in the photograph. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a benign proliferation of melanocytes that is present from birth. Compared to normal skin, within a nevus the melanocytes are clustered into nests. Nests are either located in the basal layer of the epidermis, in the dermis, or both. Compared to acquired nevi, CMN are often larger and darker. CMN are classified by their size: small (<1.5 cm), medium (1.5-20 cm), large (>20-40 cm), and giant (>40 cm). Large and giant CMN are at risk for malignant transformation. In this case, the CMN is symmetrical, uniform in color and thickness, and appears to have a rough texture. Hair is present on the inferior aspect which is common in CMN. CMN should be routinely monitored by a dermatologist. If an area within the CMN develops increased thickness or change in color, it should be biopsied to evaluate for presence of melanoma. Provided the CMN does not develop melanoma, they are benign. However, they can be associated with psychological morbidity if they are located in cosmetically sensitive areas of the body and depending on their size. Complete surgical excision of large or giant CMN is usually impossible, but particularly bothersome areas may be excised to improve function and cosmesis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hyperpigmented macula (Choice B) describe cafe-au-lait spots. A cafe-au-lait spot is characterized by a tan to dark brown, uniformly pigmented macule or patch often seen at birth or noticed in early childhood. This lesion, in contrast, is a dark brown plaque with the presence of hair at the inferior aspect. It may be asymmetrical or have an irregular border. It represents a focal increase in melanin production rather than an increased number of melanocytes or any form of malignancy. While numerous cafe-au-lait spots suggest an underlying genetic disease, a single lesion is a normal finding. Macular stain (Choice C), port-wine stain (Choice D), and superficial hemangioma (Choice E) are all vascular lesions and will appear red to purple rather than brown to black. Macular stains, or nevi flammeus, are common red patches present on the forehead and posterior neck at birth. Port-wine stain and nevus flammeus are both capillary malformations while superficial hemangioma is a benign proliferation of capillary sized vessels. These lesions are benign, but superficial hemangiomas may ulcerate and bleed. Both port-wine stains and superficial hemangiomas can be treated with laser therapy to decrease the size and color if desired. Nevus flammeus on the forehead and eyelids commonly resolves and those on the posterior neck usually fade but do not completely disappear. Educational Objective: Congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a benign proliferation of melanocytes that is present from birth. Compared to acquired nevi, CMN are often larger and darker. Hair may be present. There is an increased risk for malignant transformation in large or giant CMN and regular monitoring should be performed.

questionStem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a scaly, pruritic rash on intertriginous areas of her elbows and knees that worsens in the spring and the fall; it often appears in conjunction with episodes of respiratory distress and wheezing . Treatment with which of the following is the most effective short-term treatment of the rash?
correctExplanation: Atopic dermatitis, or eczema, is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease common in children. The diagnosis of atopic dermatitis is made based on clinical symptoms. Pruritus must be present in addition to three of the following: current or past flexural eczema, history of asthma or hay fever, or presence of dry skin within the past year. The rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting. With chronic scratching, they become dry, scaly, and excoriated in a process called lichenification. This patient's flexural dermatitis and apparent asthma and hay fever suggest a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis. Treatment of atopic dermatitis begins with gentle skin care: minimizing long baths in warm water which causes drying of the skin, avoiding products with fragrance, and use of bland moisturizers such as petroleum jelly daily. Flares of eczema are treated with mild to moderate potency topical corticosteroids, such as triamcinolone. In children, a moderate potency topical corticosteroid should not be used consistently for over 2 to 3 weeks because of the potential of systemic absorption.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Clotrimazole (Choice A) is a topical anti-fungal used to treat superficial dermatophyte infections such as tinea pedis and tinea corporis. Griseofulvin (Choice C) is a systemic antifungal used to treat tinea capitis in children. While the bacterial and fungal microbiome do play a role in the development and treatment of atopic dermatitis, triamcinolone is a more effective short-term treatment of eczema. Coal tar (Choice B) is a topical remedy used in psoriasis, not eczema. Its mechanism is not fully elucidated, but it is thought to be anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative to the epidermis. Lindane (Choice D) is an antiparasitic agent which in the past has been used to treat lice infestation. However, it is no longer used given the relatively high incidence of neurologic toxicity. This is especially of concern in young children, who have a lower body surface area to volume ratio. Educational Objective: Atopic dermatitis, or eczema, is characterized by pruritus and recurrent episodes of dermatitis on the flexural surfaces of children. It is commonly seen in concert with asthma and allergies (food or seasonal), which form the atopic triad.

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination 2 weeks after being treated for an ear infection . He has had recurrent ear infections , sinusitis , and two episodes of bacterial pneumonia since birth. Over the past year, he has undergone placement of two sets of tympanostomy tubes for otitis media. His mother is HIV negative . He currently takes no medications . He is at the 25th percentile for height and weight. Examination shows no abnormalities except for small anterior cervical lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of disease?
correctExplanation: lgA deficiency is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. Selective lgA deficiency describes a decreased or absent concentration of circulating lgA with normal concentrations of lgG, and normal or increased concentrations of lgM. lgA is critical for immune health and functions in two primary ways. First, lgA binds pathogen surface antigens targeting them for opsonization, complement activation, and phagocytosis. Second, lgA coats mucosal surfaces and prevents colonization, adhesion, and invasion by pathogenic microorganisms. lmmunoglobulins are produced by plasma cells, which are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes; as a result, most causal deficiencies are hypothesized to be related to B lymphocyte abnormalities. Despite this, there is clinical heterogeneity in the severity of lgA deficiency. Some patients remain asymptomatic while others suffer from recurrent sinopulmonary infections or otitis media, as is the case for this patient. In younger patients with severe deficiency, failure to thrive is common. Anaphylactic reactions to blood products such as plasma (which contain donor immunoglobulin) are classic but uncommon, as not all patients with lgA deficiency have reactions to blood products. Such severe reactions are most common in patients with undetectable concentrations of lgA; these reactions occur because of the presence of preformed antibodies against lgA, which is a non-native protein in these patients, and thus, a target of immune activation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Impaired chemotaxis (Choice B) describes several syndromes, one of which is hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome. These patients have abnormal Th 17 T-lymphocyte function and thus, impaired release of IL-17, a potent agent for neutrophil chemotaxis. These patients present with recurrent abscesses with minimal inflammation. Impaired respiratory burst (Choice C) describes chronic granulomatous disease, which is caused by a deficiency in NADPH oxidase, an enzyme used to generate hydrogen peroxide and hypochlorous acid. These molecules are typically used to kill bacteria intracellularly. Patients present with recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, with normal concentrations of leukocytes and immunoglobulins. Splenic dysfunction (Choice D) can be the consequence of splenectomy or can occur in diseases such as sickle cell disease, where patients become functionally asplenic early in the course of disease. This predisposes to infection with encapsulated organisms such as Haemophi/us influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. lgA deficiency is the more likely diagnosis for this patient. T-lymphocyte dysfunction (Choice E) describes numerous disorders affecting either T-lymphocyte maturation, survival, or function. Conditions such as severe combined immunodeficiency syndrome (SCIO) or Di George syndrome result in a near absence of T lymphocytes with recurrent viral and fungal infections. T lymphocytes also play a role in augmenting B-lymphocyte activation, so deficiency or dysfunction can impair humoral immunity. These patients present with severe and recurrent invasive infections early in life. Educational Objective: Selective lgA deficiency describes a decreased or absent concentration of circulating lgA, an immunoglobulin critical to mucosal immunity. Patients may be either asymptomatic or present with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, otitis media, and failure to thrive. Anaphylaxis following a blood transfusion as a result of preformed anti-lgA antibodies can also occur. lmmunoglobulin concentrations will demonstrate decreased or absent concentrations of lgA and normal or high concentrations of lgG and lgM.

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . He is active and has been healthy except for an episode of otitis media 3 weeks ago treated with amoxicillin . His parents emigrated from Vietnam . His diet consists mainly of fruits and vegetables ; he occasionally eats fish and chicken but no red meat. Examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show : Hemoglobin Mean corpuscular volume Leukocyte count Platelet count Red cell distribution width 10 g/dL 64 µm 3 6100/mm 3 225,000/mm 3 10% (N=13%-15%) A blood smear is shown . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's anemia?
correctExplanation: This asymptomatic child with mild anemia, microcytosis, and low red cell distribution width (RDW), who is of Southeast Asian heritage most likely has either a- or ~-thalassemia minor. Thalassemia is characterized by the decreased synthesis of globin chains. Normal adult hemoglobin is known as HbA (a~2l and is made of two a-globin chains and two ~-globin chains. There are four a-globin alleles and two ~-globin alleles. Mutations in one or two a-globin alleles or one ~-globin allele causes thalassemia minor. Thalassemia trait is common in Southeast Asia and presents with mild microcytic anemia. Features include the presence of target cells on peripheral blood smear (pictured in the photomicrograph above), a low RDW (which indicates that most erythrocytes are of the same size with little variation), and persistence of microcytosis. Iron concentrations can be measured to rule out iron deficiency. Other cell lines including platelets and white blood cells should be within normal ranges. Hemoglobin electrophoresis can be used to distinguish between a- and ~-thalassemia minor. There is no treatment required for thalassemia minor as the resultant anemia is usually not severe.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Antibiotic-induced autoimmune hemolysis (Choice A) can occur after exposure to penicillins and cephalosporins, but the onset is typically acute and occurs within hours to days. While hemolysis can occur weeks later, it is less common. Additionally, patients would be expected to present with normocytic anemia and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Haptoglobin concentrations can be measured and will be decreased, while the reticulocyte count will typically be increased. Iron deficiency (Choice C) is a common cause of anemia in menstruating women, strict vegans or vegetarians, and those with chronic gastrointestinal bleeding or Celiac disease. It commonly presents with microcytosis, although often with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) that is higher than what is seen in thalassemia, and an increased RDW indicating the release of premature erythrocytes, which are larger, from the bone marrow. The measurement of serum iron and ferritin are used to make the diagnosis. Transient postinfectious bone marrow suppression (Choice D) may occur following viral infections, but more commonly presents with leukopenia, which is not present in this case. In patients with sickle cell disease, infection with parvovirus B19 can cause a transient aplastic crisis and severe anemia.

questionStem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination . He has no history of serious illness . During the past 2 years , he has noticed brown urine whenever he has a cold. He has not had dysuria or urinary urgency or incontinence . Examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine C3 Urine Blood Protein 15 mg/dl 0.9 mg/dl 90 mg/dl (N=83-177) 4+ 3+ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: lgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is a type of nephritic syndrome resulting in episodic gross hematuria, often following an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal tract infection. Nephritic syndromes typically present with acute kidney injury with associated hematuria, red blood cell casts, and hypertension. On urinalysis, there will be a significant quantity of red blood cells (RBCs), possible RBC casts, and sub-nephrotic range proteinuria. Serum complement concentrations, including C3, are typically within reference ranges. This differentiates lgA nephropathy from postinfectious glomerulonephritis, which results in decreased serum C3 complement. Additionally, anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers will be negative in lgA nephropathy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hemolytic uremic syndrome {Choice A) is caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (O157:H?) and is usually accompanied by bloody diarrhea. This is characterized by a classic triad of thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Hemorrhagic cystitis {Choice B) refers to inflammation of the urinary bladder, which commonly is secondary to an acute bacterial urinary tract infection presenting with dysuria, urinary urgency, and frequency. A typical infectious cystitis presents with increased urinary white blood cells with detectable leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis, depending on the infectious organism. In hemorrhagic cystitis, red blood cells are also present on urinalysis. Nephrotic syndrome {Choice D) typically presents with excessive proteinuria (>3 g/day) hyperlipidemia, hypoalbuminemia, and peripheral edema. It does not cause hematuria. The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is minimal change disease. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis {Choice E) is a nephritic syndrome presenting with urinary RBCs and RBC casts, which typically occurs between 2 and 6 weeks after infection with group A ~-hemolytic streptococci. Results of laboratory studies will show decreased serum C3 concentrations, and anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers are positive. Educational Objective: lgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is a type of nephritic syndrome resulting in episodic gross hematuria, often following an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal tract infection. Serum complement concentrations, including C3, are typically within reference ranges.

questionStem: A 13-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive difficulty breathing . Her mother says that her daughter 's hands and feet have appeared swollen during this period . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 98/min , respirations are 30/min , and blood pressure is 124/84 mm Hg. Examination shows dusky nail beds and clubbing of the fingers and toes . There is nasal flaring and moderate intercostal retractions . Bilateral crackles and rhonchi are heard on auscultation . S2 is loud and split in the second left intercostal space . The liver edge is palpated 5 cm below the right costal margin , and the spleen tip is palpated 1 cm below the left costal margin . There is bilateral pitting edema over the dorsum of the hands and feet. Laboratory studies show : Serum Na+ CI- K+ HC0 3- Albumin Urine protein 126 mEq/L 84 mEq/L 4.1 mEq/L 36 mEq/L 2.8 g/dl 1+ Pulmonary function tests show a decrease in forced vital capacity from 75% to 30% of predicted value over the past year. An x-ray of the chest shows marked hyperinflation with coarse nodular infiltrates bilaterally . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's edema?
correctExplanation: This patient with cystic fibrosis is likely presenting with findings of volume overload in cor pulmonale. Patients with cystic fibrosis may develop pulmonary hypertension as a result of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and fibrotic remodeling in chronically hypoventilated and inflamed pulmonary parenchyma leading to increased vascular resistance. If severe, this process can lead to cor pulmonale, which refers to isolated right heart failure secondary to chronic pulmonary pathology with increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right-sided heart pressures. Right heart failure typically presents with venous congestion, seen as jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, and hepatomegaly with or without ascites.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Cirrhosis of the liver {Choice A) occurs secondary to many causes, the most common being alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Cirrhosis presents with ascites, anasarca, jaundice, increased transaminases, low albumin concentration, and impaired hepatic synthetic function. While right heart failure may cause cirrhosis, this patient only has some consistent findings. Inferior vena cava obstruction {Choice C) causes the obstruction of venous drainage from the lower regions of the body, often related to an underlying malignancy and associated mass effect, thrombosis from an indwelling catheter, or as a result of compression by a gravid uterus. This patient lacks a history suggestive of any likely cause of inferior vena cava obstruction. Lymphedema {Choice D) refers to swelling secondary to abnormal lymphatic drainage of a region, often secondary to surgery, radiation, or invasive parasitic disease. This patient lacks the appropriate history for these causes. Nephrotic syndrome {Choice E) results from many causes and typically presents with proteinuria, edema, hyperlipidemia, and a hypercoagulable state. Cystic fibrosis does not commonly cause nephrotic syndrome. Protein-losing enteropathy {Choice F) refers to any gastrointestinal pathology that results in the loss of protein, which may present with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and peripheral edema. questionStem: A 2-month -old infant has a large posterior fontanelle , a large tongue , and hypotonia. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation; pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of disease?
correctExplanation: Congenital thyroid dysfunction that leads to hypothyroidism is typically asymptomatic at birth. This is because maternal thyroid hormone is able to cross the placenta, which keeps the newborn in a euthyroid state. Congenital hypothyroidism commonly presents in the first few months of life with feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, hypotonia, and hypothermia. Infants with this disorder may also present with goiter, or congenital cardiac, kidney, or gastrointestinal malformations. Thyroid dysfunction can be caused by a variety of mechanisms, including thyroid dysgenesis, resistance to thyroid-stimulating hormone, abnormalities in thyroid hormone transport, iodine deficiency, maternal antibodies, or antithyroid medications. Congenital hypothyroidism is now typically identified on routine newborn screening. It is treated with thyroid hormone supplementation (eg, levothyroxine) but can lead to intellectual disability or neurologic issues (eg, hearing loss, ataxia) if untreated.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Anterior horn cell degeneration (Choice A) is seen in spinal muscular atrophy, which presents with hypotonia and weakness in the newborn. It can also present with a weak cry, difficulty feeding, and respiratory failure, which are not seen in this patient. Connective tissue disorders (Choice B) include Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndrome. These are not typically apparent at birth, rather manifesting later as hyperflexiblity and skin elasticity (Ehlers-Danlos) or tall stature with long extremities and fingers (Marfan syndrome). They are not associated with macroglossia or a large posterior fontanelle. Cortical dysfunction (Choice C) can occur secondary to cerebral palsy, intracranial hemorrhage, or a variety of other neurologic conditions. It would be expected to present more broadly with intellectual disability or developmental delay, as well neuromuscular abnormalities such as unilateral weakness or spastic paralysis. Electrolyte imbalances (Choice D) can lead to cardiac irritability (potassium, magnesium, calcium), skeletal abnormalities (calcium), altered mental status or neurologic abnormalities (sodium, calcium), and neuromuscular weakness (potassium, magnesium). Changes in electrolyte concentrations would not be expected to present with a large posterior fontanelle and tongue. Myopathy (Choice E) generally presents with muscle weakness, rather than hypotonia, although the latter can also be present. If present at 2 months of age, the diagnosis would likely be congenital myopathy. Depending on the subtype, congenital myopathies can present with a variety of symptoms and anatomic abnormalities, such as respiratory failure or scoliosis, although these do not include a large posterior fontanelle or macroglossia. Peripheral neuropathy (Choice F) commonly presents with paresthesias, numbness, or weakness in the extremities, and it can be caused by congenital disorders, diabetes mellitus, injury, or infection. It would not be expected to present with a large posterior fontanelle and tongue. Spinal cord dysfunction (Choice G) could present with weakness, numbness, paresthesias, or autonomic instability. However, it would be unlikely to cause anatomic changes superior to the area of dysfunction. Educational Objective: Congenital hypothyroidism presents in the first few months of life with feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, hypotonia, and hypothermia.

questionStem: An 18-year-old man has had nausea, fatigue , and periorbital swelling for 4 days; the swelling is worse in the morning . He had tonsillitis 2 weeks ago that resolved after treatment with penicillin . His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 170/95 mm Hg. There is periorbital edema bilaterally and trace ankle edema . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A Acute renal failure
correctExplanation: Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Urine Protein WBC RBC RBC casts 60 mg/dl 4 mg/dl 1+ few many 1/hpf This patient presents with acute renal failure following a tonsillar infection, consistent with a diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), a nephritic syndrome. PSGN typically occurs between 2 and 4 weeks following an acute infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) (typically impetigo, streptococcal pharyngitis, or tonsillitis). Appropriate treatment of the streptococcal infection with antibiotics does not reduce the likelihood of subsequently developing PSGN. PSGN is caused by a type Ill hypersensitivity reaction with the kidney deposition of immune complexes and complement. Patients typically present with dark­ colored urine, hypertension, and peripheral and periorbital edema. Urinalysis typically shows red blood cell casts. The diagnosis is confirmed with kidney biopsy, which shows enlarged glomeruli on light microscopy, bumpy irregularity of the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence, and subepithelial immune complex deposits on electron microscopy. Treatment is supportive and includes diuretics and antihypertensive agents.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Biventricular heart failure (Choice B) may occur in severe cases of myocarditis or rheumatic heart disease. Heart failure would not cause hematuria and red blood cell casts, which is more suggestive of a nephritic syndrome. Cirrhosis of the liver (Choice C) occurs secondary to many causes, the most common being alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Cirrhosis presents with ascites, anasarca, jaundice, increased transaminases, decreased albumin, and impaired hepatic synthetic function. It does not occur following streptococcal infections and does not usually present with hypertension or hematuria. Inferior vena cava obstruction (Choice D) prevents venous drainage from the inferior regions of the body, often related to an underlying malignancy and associated mass effect, thrombosis from an indwelling catheter, or as a result of compression by a gravid uterus. This patient lacks a history suggestive of any likely cause of inferior vena cava obstruction. Nephrotic syndrome (Choice E) results from many causes and typically presents with proteinuria, edema, hyperlipidemia, and a hypercoagulable state. PSGN is a primarily nephritic process and usually results in mild, sub-nephrotic range proteinuria. Educational Objective: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis can cause acute renal failure following an acute infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) (typically impetigo, streptococcal pharyngitis, tonsillitis). Patients present with dark-colored urine, hypertension, and peripheral and periorbital edema; urinalysis shows red blood casts.

questionStem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of vaginal bleeding for 12 hours. She has a 3-month history of a purulent vaginal discharge . Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 1. Examination shows a purulent bloody discharge on her underwear . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: Vaginal foreign bodies can present in prepubertal children with genital discomfort, vulvar erythema, vaginal discharge, or vaginal bleeding. The most common foreign body is toilet paper, but other objects such as small toy parts and coins may be inserted as a result of the child's curiosity and exploratory genital play. Diagnosis with visualization of the vaginal vault, saline irrigation, or examination under anesthesia may be required. Treatment requires removal of the foreign body.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Central lesion causing precocious puberty (Choice A) can occur with craniopharyngiomas, gliomas, or other central nervous system tumors. It is rare and would present with signs of precocious puberty including breast and pubic hair development, growth acceleration, and voice changes. Isolated menarche (Choice B) describes vaginal bleeding in a prepubertal child in which no secondary causes have been identified, such as precocious puberty, infection, foreign bodies, trauma, or tumors. In a patient with purulent and bloody vaginal discharge, the presence of a foreign body is more likely. Vulvovaginitis (Choice C) involves the overgrowth of normal vaginal Candida flora, bacterial vaginosis, or Trichomonas vaginitis. Candida as a cause of vulvovaginitis can be distinguished from other causes by abnormal, often white, vaginal discharge with normal vaginal pH, negative KOH testing, and the absence of motile trichomonads on wet mount preparation. Risk factors for Candida vulvovaginitis include the use of medications, especially antibiotics, or an immunocompromised state. It would be unlikely in this child with none of these risk factors. Vaginal tumors (Choice E) can include squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, adenocarcinoma, and sarcoma. Rhabdomyosarcoma is a rare, aggressive malignancy formed by striated muscle cells. It is found in children and can present as a genitourinary mass with hematuria, urinary tract obstruction, or a protruding vaginal mass. Educational Objective: Vaginal foreign bodies can present in prepubertal children with genital discomfort, vulvar erythema, vaginal discharge, or vaginal bleeding. While sexual abuse should be considered, vaginal foreign bodies are more common as a result of a child's curiosity and exploratory genital play.

questionStem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 10 minutes after he was found coughing and choking near an open can of peanuts . His parents attempted a Heimlich maneuver , but his condition did not improve . On arrival , he is agitated and unable to speak because of shortness of breath . His pulse is 150/min, respirations are 35/min , and blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg. Examination shows intercostal and suprasternal retractions . There are wheezes and poor air movement on the right. An expiratory x-ray of the chest is shown . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.B: Complete obstruction and collapse of the left lung
choices.D: Partial obstruction of the right main stem bronchus

correctExplanation: The patient likely has a partial obstruction of the right main stem bronchus as a result of foreign body aspiration. The chest plain film shows air trapping on the right-side during expiration suggesting a blockage of the bronchus. The left side shows increased interstitial markings as expected during expiration. The impaired gas exchange and resistance to airflow results in dyspnea, tachypnea, and increased respiratory effort. Air moving through a narrowed lumen generates a wheeze. The right main stem bronchus is the most common site of foreign body aspiration as it is wider and more vertically aligned than the left main stem bronchus. Patients at risk include young children and patients with altered mental status, impaired cough reflex, and impaired swallowing.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aspiration pneumonia on the left (Choice A) would be suggested if there were increased interstitial markings on the left side compared to the right during an inspiratory chest x-ray. Aspiration pneumonia may be caused by infection from oropharyngeal microbes. Complete obstruction and collapse of the left lung (Choice B) would appear as reduced volume on the left side with ipsilateral mediastinal shift caused by pressure from the compensatory hyperinflation of the right side. This expiratory film is more suggestive of a right bronchus obstruction, which is a more common site for foreign body aspiration. Obstruction of the midtrachea (Choice C) can be life-threatening because of disruption of air flow to both lungs. Obstructions in the trachea often present with stridor, a distinct high-pitched respiratory sound associated with abnormal laryngeal or tracheal air flow. Pneumothorax on the right (Choice E) is incorrect, as lung markings are present out to the periphery in the plain film. Spontaneous pneumothorax is more common in tall, thin males. Educational Objective: Partial obstruction of the airways, whether caused by foreign body aspiration or an obstructive pulmonary disease state, may be evaluated by contrasting inspiratory chest imaging with expiratory imaging. Obstruction is worsened by positive intrathoracic pressure during expiration, which results in air trapping in the affected lung segment.

questionStem: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 2-hour history of increasing headache , dizziness , and nausea . His father is a butcher and says his son ate a new batch of sausage shortly before he became ill. Earlier today, the patient was given the task of cleaning out the garage . On arrival , the patient is alert and is not in respiratory distress . His pulse is 136/min, respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 104/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 73% that increases to 80% when 15 L/min of oxygen is administered via face mask. Examination shows profound central cyanosis . The pupils are equal and reactive to light. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . His methemoglobin is 40.5% of his total hemoglobin . Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows : Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: 7.37 42 mm Hg 48 mm Hg 24 mEq/L Methemoglobinemia occurs when an abnormal fraction of heme iron in the blood exists in the ferric (Fe3•) form (methemoglobin). Methemoglobin cannot effectively bind oxygen, which impairs tissue oxygen delivery. Most cases of methemoglobinemia are acquired, typically via exposure to an oxidant stressor such as an anesthetic (eg, benzocaine), nitrate, or dapsone. Symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue, lethargy, lightheadedness, and in severe cases, arrhythmia, seizure, and multisystem organ failure. Vital signs typically show reduced oxygen saturation, and examination may disclose cyanosis. Characteristically, blood appears darkened on gross visualization, although hemoglobin concentration and erythrocyte morphology are normal. Treatment includes supplemental oxygen plus the intravenous administration of methylene blue, a reducing agent that donates electrons to heme. The reduction of heme iron to the ferrous (Fe2•) form restores the ability of hemoglobin to bind, carry, and deliver oxygen to tissues.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Administration of atropine (Choice A) would be indicated in cases of symptomatic bradycardia or organophosphate poisoning. This patient's pulse is tachycardic and atropine administration would be inappropriate. Administration of deferoxamine (Choice B) is indicated in the treatment of hemochromatosis or iron toxicity. It is a therapy that binds free iron in the serum and promotes elimination in the urine. Administration of naloxone (Choice D) is indicated in cases of opioid overdose. Opioid overdoses are characterized by respiratory depression presenting as a decreased respiratory rate, apnea, and hypoxia. This patient's hypoxia is caused by methemoglobinemia, not respiratory depression. Administration of pyridostigmine (Choice E) is used in the treatment of myasthenia gravis. It is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases the concentration of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (Choice F) can be helpful in the treatment of decompression sickness and carbon monoxide poisoning. Educational Objective: Methemoglobinemia occurs when an abnormal fraction of heme iron in the blood exists in the ferric (Fe3•) form (methemoglobin). The treatment of methemoglobinemia includes supplemental oxygen plus the intravenous administration of methylene blue, a reducing agent that donates electrons to heme. The reduction of heme iron to the ferrous (Fe 2•) form restores the ability of hemoglobin to bind, carry, and deliver oxygen to tissues.

questionStem: A 10-day-old male newborn is admitted to the hospital for treatment of indirect hyperbilirubinemia due to isoimmune hemolysis . He is placed in a room with a 2-month-old female infant with dehydration secondary to rotavirus gastroenteritis . Two days later, he develops vomiting and diarrhea , and a stool specimen is positive for rotavirus antigen . This nosocomial infection is most likely caused by failure of caregivers to do which of the following?

choices.A: Dispose of diapers and other waste items properly
choices.D: Place the patients in a reverse airflow room

correctExplanation: Observation of proper hand-washing techniques is the most effective strategy to limit the spread of nosocomial enteric viral pathogens. Viral shedding in the stool can occur prior to the development of symptoms and potentially allow asymptomatic patients to become vectors for disease. Additionally, viral shedding in the stool persists until after the resolution of symptoms. Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not as efficacious at removing enteric viruses from the hands or other commonly touched surfaces, although cleaning agents that utilize bleach are effective. It is likely that the 10-day-old newborn acquired rotavirus infection after caregivers came in contact with a surface contaminated by feces from the 2-month-old infant and then touched the younger child without washing their hands properly. Spread of enteric viruses can be reduced by simply by performing routine hand washing, which typically involves rubbing the hands together with soap for at least twenty seconds. Individuals often neglect to scrub the entire surface of the hand despite an adequate duration of hand washing.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Disposing of diapers and other waste items properly (Choice A) is also important, as rotavirus is shed in the stool, but adherence to these measures tends to be higher amongst caregivers than the simple observance of hand washing. It is unlikely that the patient acquired infection directly through contact with the other patient's diapers; caregivers more likely touched other contaminated surfaces. Observing gown and glove precautions (Choice B) is an important part of preventing the spread of certain bacteria and viruses, and contact precautions are often instituted in instances of viral gastroenteritis. However, proper hand washing should always occur before and after donning and doffing gown and gloves. Placing the patient in a reverse airflow room (Choice D) would have little effect on the transmission of rotavirus as this pathogen is not transmitted by aerosolized particles. Negative pressure rooms are more commonly reserved for airborne pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and measles, among others. Restricting visitors to the room (Choice E) decreases the number of individuals who can potentially act as vectors to transfer rotavirus between the patients, but observing proper hand washing is more likely to reduce the spread of infection regardless of the number of visitors. Educational Objective: Proper hand-washing technique includes rubbing the hands together with soap for at least twenty seconds before rinsing. It is common for individuals to neglect to scrub the entire surface of the hands. Hand washing is more efficacious in preventing the spread of enteric pathogens than any other preventive measure and should be observed judiciously.

questionStem: A previously healthy 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of fever and enlarged lymph nodes for 3 weeks . He has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss over the past 2 months. He has had six to eight loose stools daily for 4 weeks . His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 80/min , and respirations are 30/min . Examination shows dry skin. There are bilateral 2-cm lymph nodes in the neck, axillae , and groin. The lungs are clear to auscultation . The liver edge is palpated 1 cm below the right costal margin ; the spleen tip is palpated 7 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Lymphocytes Monocytes Platelet count Serum lgA lgG lgM 10 g/dL 2100/mm 3 80% 18% 2% 180,000/mm 3 340 mg/dL 2300 mg/dL 390 mg/dL This patient with generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly with leukopenia most likely has acute HIV infection, known as acute retroviral syndrome. The presentation of primary HIV infection can vary significantly between patients, with some experiencing a mild febrile illness while others experience a severe, mononucleosis-like viral syndrome. The time between infection and onset of symptoms is variable, with incubation time lasting several weeks to months. During acute infection, there is a high degree of viral replication followed by widespread infection of CD4+ T lymphocytes. While the T­ lymphocyte count may decrease transiently, it is often within reference ranges in early HIV infection unless patients present with signs of opportunistic infection. Initial laboratory studies include the use of a fourth generation HIV test, which tests for HIV p24 antigen and antibodies, combined with direct measurement of the HIV viral load using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction testing. It is common in early infection for patients to have a negative fourth generation test but a high viral load; this is known as the window period. Once the diagnosis is made, laboratory studies should be sent for mutational analysis and genotyping, but this should not delay immediate treatment with antiretroviral therapy. Therapy typically includes a combination of at least three different medications from at least two different antiretroviral classes.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Common variable immunodeficiency (Choice A) classically presents between the ages of 20 to 40 years as multiple, recurrent sinus or pulmonary infections, including pneumonia, bronchitis, and sinusitis. Testing will disclose low immunoglobulin concentrations. Selective lgA deficiency (Choice C) describes an absence of lgA with normal concentrations of lgG, and normal or increased concentrations of lgM. Many patients are asymptomatic and do not demonstrate a history of recurrent infections. The classic presentation is anaphylaxis after transfusion of blood products, which occurs as the result of pre-formed anti-lgA antibodies. Severe combined immunodeficiency (Choice D) results from a variety of different mutations and commonly presents with recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections as a result of severe impairment in both B­ and T-lymphocyte function in infancy. questionStem: Two hours after delivery at term, a newborn has a blood glucose concentration of 25 mg/dl. Pregnancy was complicated by poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus . He is at the 70th percentile for length and 90th percentile for weight. Examination shows plethora . Which of the following is the most likely primary mechanism of the blood glucose concentration?
correctExplanation: Excessive fetal exposure to insulin in utero can cause macrosomia, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, and hypoglycemia in the newborn. Human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance. This leads to increased concentrations of glucose in the maternal circulation, and subsequently the fetal circulation. Fetal hyperglycemia in turn causes the fetus to produce excess insulin, with a consequent decrease in the rate of gluconeogenesis. The insulin then acts as a growth factor, leading to macrosomia, and inhibits the production of surfactant, which leads to respiratory distress syndrome. After birth, the fetus continues to synthesize insulin but is no longer exposed to maternal blood glucose concentrations, leading to hypoglycemia. Treatment is supportive and includes administration of supplemental glucose while neonatal endocrine regulation self-corrects.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Decreased gluconeogenesis (Choice A) will occur in this newborn with chronic exposure to insulin in utero. However, the underlying mechanism for the decreased gluconeogenesis is increased insulin secretion. Decreased insulin secretion (Choice B) is seen in diabetes mellitus and would lead to hyperglycemia. Type 1 diabetes mellitus does not commonly present in the newborn; it more commonly presents in children with polyuria, polydipsia, or diabetic ketoacidosis. Increased glucagon secretion (Choice C) would cause neonatal hyperglycemia, as its main mechanism of action is to increase plasma glucose. Eventually, glucagon secretion will increase, and insulin secretion will decrease, which will return the blood glucose concentrations to normal reference ranges. Increased gluconeogenesis (Choice D) would increase the plasma glucose concentration and would occur with increased glucagon. This patient is presenting with hypoglycemia as a result of excessive insulin secretion. Insulin resistance (Choice F) would present with hyperglycemia and is seen in type 2 diabetes mellitus. This more commonly presents later in life in obese, sedentary patients, and would not be expected in a newborn. Educational Objective: Maternal diabetes mellitus exposes a fetus to increased concentrations of blood glucose, in response to which the fetus increases production of insulin and consequently decreases gluconeogenesis. Following birth, this can lead to postnatal hypoglycemia as the newborn is no longer exposed to increased concentrations of blood glucose in the maternal circulation.

questionStem: A 6-hour-old female newborn has had cyanosis of her arms and legs since birth. She was born at 38 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and cesarean delivery for breech presentation . She weighed 3090 g (6 lb 13 oz) at birth. She has been breast-feeding well. She is alert and is not in acute distress . Her rectal temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 80/45 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Examination shows cyanosis of the upper and lower extremities but no circumoral cyanosis . Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . Capillary refill time is mildly delayed . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Placement of the newborn under warming lights

correctExplanation: This neonate has a slightly decreased body temperature of 36.2°C (97.2°F) while her other vital signs are within normal limits for a neonate. Cyanosis of the extremities and delayed capillary refill time are manifestations of mild hypothermia. Neonates, particularly preterm neonates, have a high body surface area relative to their mass which makes them prone to rapid heat loss and the development of hypothermia. Neonatal hypothermia requires prompt correction as it is associated with increased mortality. Hypothermia increases oxygen consumption and metabolic demands on the neonate which leads to less successful resuscitation efforts if they are needed. Interventions directed at temperature regulation immediately after delivery include increasing the temperature of the delivery room, placing the neonate in skin-to-skin contact with its mother immediately after birth, using a radiant heater during resuscitation, and swaddling after drying.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hypothermia can be a sign of systemic illness, such as sepsis, but in this neonate with relatively mild hypothermia and an otherwise normal course in the first 6 hours after delivery, systemic illness is unlikely. Blood culture (Choice B) is unnecessary. This infant is mildly cyanotic in the extremities because of the vasoconstrictive response to the cold environment, not as a result of respiratory distress or a congenital heart defect. Respirations of 36/min and an oxygen saturation of 96% are within normal limits, and cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Thus, neither a chest x-ray (Choice C) nor intubation and mechanical ventilation (Choice E) are needed at this time. Likewise, there is nothing to suggest a congenital heart defect as the cause of her cyanosis, so an echocardiography (Choice D) is not needed at this time. Educational Objective: Neonatal hypothermia may develop after delivery as a result of rapid heat loss of the neonate. Cyanosis of the extremities and delayed capillary refill time are manifestations of such. Neonatal hypothermia requires prompt correction as it is associated with increased mortality.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and increasingly severe headache and malaise. He has a history of recurrent pneumonia ; the last episode was 2 years ago. His family recently immigrated to the USA from Mexico. On arrival, he is somnolent but arousable . His temperature is 39.3°C (102.8°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 146/94 mm Hg. Examination shows nuchal rigidity. Crackles are heard over the left lower lung field. On mental status examination , he is oriented to person but not to place or time. A lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows: Opening pressure 340 mm HP Glucose 28 mg/dL Total protein 154 mg/dL Leukocyte count 8648/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 85% Lymphocytes 15% Erythrocyte count 95/mm 3 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Meningitis presents with fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status, typically following a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms, although it can also be concomitant with another infection. It is caused by bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens, although bacterial pathogens usually cause the most acute and severe illness. Physical examination will commonly show a positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign, indicative of meningeal irritation, and can also disclose focal neurologic symptoms or signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as hemiparesis or a sixth cranial nerve palsy. Results of laboratory studies will show leukocytosis, and coagulation studies can show signs of disseminated intravascular coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia, decreased fibrinogen, and increased □-dimer, depending on the specific pathogen. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation is the initial diagnostic step and will show an increased opening pressure, increased white blood cell count with prominent neutrophils, increased protein concentration, and decreased glucose concentration in bacterial meningitis. Culture of the CSF is utilized to diagnose the specific bacterial cause. The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in children and young adults is Streptococcus pneumoniae, although its incidence has decreased with the pneumococcal vaccine. Risk factors for its development include an immunocompromised state, diabetes mellitus, and chronic heart or lung disease. Treatment involves immediate antibiotic therapy, accompanied by glucocorticoids.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Cryptococcal meningitis {Choice A) is a fungal meningitis that occurs most commonly in immunocompromised patients, such as those with lymphoma, leukemia, HIV/AIDS, or solid organ transplantation. Cryptococcus neoformans can also cause encephalitis and pulmonary cryptococcosis. However, fungal meningitis will show prominent lymphocytes on CSF evaluation, rather than a predominance of neutrophils, as in this patient. Enterovirus meningitis {Choice B) more commonly occurs in patients less than one year of age but can present in children and young adults. Viral meningitis is associated with a normal opening pressure, predominance of lymphocytes, and normal protein and glucose concentrations on CSF evaluation. Herpes simplex encephalitis {Choice C) presents in patients of all ages with fever, headache, seizures, focal neurologic signs, and confusion. Herpes simplex is commonly associated with a significant amount of red blood cells on CSF evaluation, as well as neuroimaging that shows inflammation in the temporal lobe. Neurocysticercosis {Choice D) is an infection caused by the parasitic pork tapeworm Taenia solium that occurs most commonly in endemic rural regions of Latin America, Asia, and Africa. questionStem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever, progressive cough, and sputum production . Examination at birth showed no abnormalities , but she has a history of respiratory problems since infancy. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 32/min . Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. Examination shows clubbing , circumoral cyanosis , and a hyperexpanded chest. There are diffuse rhonchi bilaterally with end-expiratory wheezing . An x-ray of the chest shows hyperinflation , scattered atelectasis , and chronic interstitial changes . CorrectAnswer: D. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the CFTR gene, leading to a deficiency in a chloride channel that secretes chloride in the lungs and gastrointestinal tract and reabsorbs chloride in sweat glands. This abnormal chloride transport causes decreased chloride and water secretion and increased water reabsorption, leading to abnormally viscous mucous. The thick mucus in the gastrointestinal tract contributes to pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, and malabsorption, leading to a deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. In the lungs, the disease manifests as recurrent pneumonia, especially with Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Repeat antibiotic exposure increases the risk for colonization with resistant organisms. Obstruction and destruction of the airways leads to hypoxemia, air trapping, and bronchiectasis. Physical examination may disclose hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (clubbing), cyanosis, rales and rhonchi, and hyperresonance to percussion of the chest. X-ray findings include hyperinflation, bronchiectasis with peribronchial cuffing, and diffuse nonspecific inflammatory changes. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, F, G, H, I, J, and K. Asthma (Choice A) is characterized by reversible obstruction to airflow caused by the spasm of smooth muscle in the small airways. It is often triggered by an allergen (eg, smoke, pollen), exercise, or temperature change. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (Choice B) is a neonatal lung disorder associated with oxygen exposure and mechanical ventilation in preterm infants. The lungs fail to mature properly, and patients develop chronic lung disease characterized by decreased lung volumes, hyperinflation, and atelectasis. Congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt (Choice C) may be caused by tetralogy of Fallo!, transposition of the great arteries, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, or the development of Eisenmenger syndrome from reversal of a left-to-right shunt. A right-to-left shunt would be noted on examination at birth if present. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Choice E) is a congenital heart condition characterized by myocardial thickening and left outflow tract obstruction. Patients typically present with a murmur and may develop diastolic dysfunction. Idiopathic pulmonary hypertension (Choice F) is a rare pulmonary disorder with an unknown cause characterized by progressive pulmonary vascular hypertension. Persistent pulmonary hypertension (Choice I) with any cause may result in right heart failure. Patients typically present with exertional dyspnea and physical examination findings suggestive of right heart failure. Methemoglobinemia (Choice G) is the accumulation of hemoglobin with an oxidized iron atom that is unable to transport oxygen, resulting in hypoxia. Infants are more susceptible than adults. It is associated with exposure to an oxidizing agent. Patent foramen ovale (Choice H) is a common form of atrial septal defect that is typically asymptomatic but can result in a left-to-right shunt and potential for systemic embolization of venous thromboses. In the lungs, the disease manifests as recurrent pneumonia, especially with Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. X-ray findings include hyperinflation, bronchiectasis with peribronchial cuffing, and diffuse nonspecific inflammatory changes.

Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 26/min , and blood pressure is 80/46 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 87%. The lungs are clear to auscultation . There is a heave at the left sternal border. A grade 3/6, harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border with radiation to the axilla .
