questionStem: A previously healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of difficulty breathing 10 minutes after being stung by a bee. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 28/min , and blood pressure is 65/50 mm Hg. Examination shows wheezing , audible stridor, and a generalized urticaria! rash. Epinephrine and methylprednisolone are administered . Administration of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Anaphylactic shock, a severe type 1 hypersensitivity reaction, presents following exposure to an allergen. It is caused by widespread lgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and is characterized by histaminergic responses within multiple organ systems leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodilation, which can lead to airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. If not managed promptly, death can occur from hypoxia or distributive shock. Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock, which is characterized by a primary reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This reduction in SVR is secondary to lgE-mediated histamine and cytokine release. Cardiac output increases to compensate for low SVR in the early stages of distributive shock. If the inciting state is not appropriately treated, further decompensation can occur, resulting in progressive hypotension and insufficient perfusion with associated end-organ damage. After the administration of epinephrine, fluid resuscitation should be initiated to increase intravascular volume to support adequate organ perfusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cromolyn sodium (Choice A) is a therapy that prevents mast cell degranulation and the release of histamine from mast cells. It can be used in the treatment of asthma and allergic rhinitis. It is not used in anaphylaxis. Dopamine (Choice B) can be used in cases of shock or refractory hypotension. It may theoretically prevent splanchnic vasoconstriction caused by Dr and D:, receptor agonism, however this has not been well demonstrated in clinical practice. Intravenous fluids should be administered first, prior to vasopressor therapy, to support adequate organ perfusion. Lidocaine (Choice D) can be used as an antiarrhythmic agent as a result of its blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels. It is also useful for local anesthesia. Norepinephrine (Choice E) is a catecholamine similar to epinephrine that increases systemic vascular resistance. Intramuscular epinephrine is the first-line therapy for anaphylaxis; other vasopressors can be considered if the patient continues to be in shock despite maximal epinephrine therapy and fluid resuscitation. Educational Objective: Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock, which is characterized by a primary reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR). First line therapy involves epinephrine and fluid resuscitation to increase SVR and intravascular volume to support adequate organ perfusion.

questionStem: A 2-year-old girl is brought for a follow-up examination 2 days after initiating amoxicillin therapy for a right lower lobe pneumonia . She had been healthy prior to onset of the pneumonia . She continues to have fevers and cough , and she now has right-sided chest pain. Her immunizations are up-to-date . She appears ill and is tachypneic . Her temperature is 38.5°C (101 .3°F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 45/min . Repeat x-rays of the chest show a large dense consolidation in the right lower lung field and a fixed right-sided effusion . Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Pneumonia in patients under the age of 5 is a common cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Causative organisms in the pediatric population depend on the age of the patient. In the neonatal period, patients are at risk for infection from microbes present in the vaginal canal including Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. In patients between the ages of 2 and 5 years, viral pneumonia is most common. Bacterial pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Staphylococcus aureus. The risk for H. influenzae type b infection is reduced in patients with up-to-date immunizations. Staphylococcus aureus commonly expresses beta-lactamases, which confer resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics such as amoxicillin, and combination therapy with a beta-lactam or a beta-lactamase inhibitor (eg, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid) is recommended. Pneumonia may be complicated by a parapneumonic effusion, which should be evaluated by thoracentesis.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Enterobacter cloacae (Choice A) is a Gram-negative, facultative anaerobe that makes up normal gut flora. It is associated with skin and soft tissue, urinary tract, and respiratory infections, especially in immunocompromised patients. It would be an unusual cause of pneumonia in this otherwise healthy patient. Haemophi/us influenzae type b (Choice B) is an encapsulated, Gram-negative coccobacillus and a common cause of pneumonia in the pediatric and adult populations. Areas with widespread childhood immunization have significantly lower risk for contracting H. influenzae pneumonia. Mycobacterium avium-intracel/ulare (Choice C) is a non-tuberculosis acid-fast bacillus that may cause pneumonia when organisms are inhaled from the environment. Severe and disseminated disease can occur in immunocompromised patients. Staphylococcus aureus is a more common cause of pneumonia. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Choice D) is a Gram-negative bacillus ubiquitous in the environment. It can result in numerous clinical infectious conditions, including urinary tract infections, osteomyelitis, otitis externa, folliculitis, hospital or ventilator-associated pneumonia, and sepsis. Pseudomonas pneumonia is associated with cystic fibrosis. Educational Objective: Pneumonia is common in the pediatric population, and is typically caused by respiratory viruses, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Staphylococcus aureus. Immunization programs against Haemophilus influenzae type b have reduced the prevalence of this disease.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy who plays soccer has the acute onset of fever, malaise , and pain in his left lower extremity. He is unable to walk. He appears ill. His temperature is 39.4 °C (103°F). He has limited movement of the lower extremity and swelling and point tenderness over the proximal medial lower leg. There is no overlying contusion or break in the skin. His hemoglobin concentration is 12 g/dl , leukocyte count is 14,000/mm 3, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 60 mm/h. A technetium 99m bone scan shows uptake at the metaphysis of the tibia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone and bone marrow, and typically presents acutely, subacutely, or chronically from direct inoculation or hematogenous spread from a distal site. Acute osteomyelitis is more common in children and is most often caused by infection with Staphylococcus aureus. Risk factors include traumatic inoculating injury, diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, intravenous substance use, and prosthetic devices or indwelling hardware. Patients typically complain of pain, difficulty bearing weight, and overlying erythema. Laboratory studies may show leukocytosis and increased inflammatory markers. Imaging typically shows localized osseous erosive changes. Bone scintigraphy with the radiotracer technetium 99m may show increased uptake in the area of infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Osgood-Schlatter disease (Choice B) refers to osteochondrosis or traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle that typically occurs in adolescent, athletic children . This presents with progressive pain along the anterior aspect of the proximal tibia and knee that is exacerbated by kneeling. Physical examination typically discloses tenderness over an enlarged tibial tubercle. Patients do not present with inability to bear weight or fever. Fracture of the tibia (Choice C) presents with acute pain, inability to bear weight on the extremity, and localized edema and tenderness in the area of injury. Fever, leukocytosis, and increased inflammatory markers would be unusual. Bone scintigraphy may be useful for detecting occult fractures, but x-ray or CT scan would be the initial modality of choice. Prepatellar bursitis (Choice D) refers to inflammation of the bursa overlying the patella. Common causes include infection, trauma, and recurrent pressure (as from occupations that require frequent kneeling). A bone scan would show no abnormalities. Septic arthritis (Choice E) results from bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly by S. aureus. The affected joint demonstrates pain, swelling, and erythema. Arthrocentesis is indicated for the evaluation of monoarticular erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically shows purulent synovial fluid with >50,000 WBC/mm 3• Physical examination would disclose a tender, erythematous, and edematous joint, which is not present in this case. Educational Objective: Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone or bone marrow that may be caused by direct local spread of an infection or hematogenous seeding from a distal site. Patients present with fever, localized pain and inflammation, and increased inflammatory markers. Imaging may show inflammatory and destructive bony changes.

questionStem: A 6-day-old girl is brought to the physician because of vomiting for 2 days . She has not had fever. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy , labor, and delivery. Results of newborn screening are pending . She was discharged at the age of 1 day. She is exclusively breast-fed and is feeding every 3 hours. She is at the 50th percentile for length and head circumference and 5th percentile for weight. Examination shows generalized jaundice . The liver is enlarged and firm. Her serum total bilirubin concentration is 14 mg/dL , with a direct component of 8 mg/dl. Test of the urine for reducing substances is positive . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
correctExplanation: Galactosemia is the most likely diagnosis in this exclusively breast-fed patient with hepatomegaly and the presence of reducing substances in the urine. Normal metabolism of lactose involves separation into glucose and galactose by lactase. Free glucose can be used for cellular energy production while galactose must be converted to galactose-1-phosphate by galactokinase and then subsequently converted to UDP-galactose and then glucose-1-phosphate by galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). While galactosemia can result from deficiencies in several different enzymes in this pathway, deficiency of GALT causes classic galactosemia, which is an autosomal recessive disorder. Breast milk contains galactose, which patients with galactosemia are unable to break down. Early complications include jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly, diarrhea, lethargy, and occasionally sepsis with Gram-negative organisms. Coagulopathy and easy bruising may also occur. Diagnosis is made by assessing for the presence and activity of GALT in erythrocytes by radioimmunoassay. Reducing substances are molecules that can convert cupric to cuprous ions in the urine and include glucose, lactose, pentose, and galactose. The presence of these substances (galactose) can suggest the diagnosis but is not specific. Additionally, while galactosemia is detected on newborn screening, manifestations of the disease can occur before the results of screening are available. Treatment requires eliminating dietary galactose and providing necessary supplements, however, this may not reverse neurologic sequelae of the disease, such as infantile cataracts and intellectual disability.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hereditary fructose intolerance (Choice B) is caused by a deficiency in aldolase B, an enzyme important in the metabolism of fructose. Deficiency results in increased concentrations offructose-1-phosphate and fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, causing a deficiency of available phosphate, which inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Patients present with hypoglycemia only after fructose is introduced into the diet. Mucopolysaccharidosis II (Choice C), also known as Hunter syndrome, is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency in iduronate-2-sulfatase, which results in the deposition of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Within the first year of life, patients develop coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, hernias, and dysostosis multiplex. Type I glycogen storage disease (Choice D) is caused by glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency. This enzyme is located in the liver and functions in gluconeogenesis to convert glucose-6-phosphate to glucose for its release into the blood. Impaired gluconeogenesis can lead to severe hypoglycemia during periods of fasting. It is characterized by excess glycogen in the liver, hepatomegaly, and fasting hypoglycemia. Tyrosinemia (Choice E) can refer to one of several disorders in which enzymes required for the metabolism of tyrosine are deficient. In its most severe form, it can present with liver disease and renal tubular acidosis, but hypophosphatemia, bone mineralization disorders, and aminoaciduria are also potential findings. Educational Objective: Galactosemia refers to defects in enzymes that metabolize galactose. Classic galactosemia results from the deficiency of GALT, which converts galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose and then glucose-1-phosphate. Early manifestations include jaundice, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and sepsis. Reducing substances in the urine are often present but not specific.

questionStem: A 2-hour-old newborn has a large fluctuant area of swelling in the left parietal region. She was born at term following a difficult forceps delivery. The newborn is alert and in no distress . Examination of the area shows margins limited by suture lines. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the swelling?

choices.B: Blood under the periosteum of the parietal bone
choices.C: Cerebrospinal fluid under the galea aponeurotica
choices.D: Cerebrospinal fluid under the periosteum of the parietal bone

correctExplanation: Cephalohematomas are traumatic subperiosteal hematomas that can occur with uncomplicated or assisted vaginal deliveries. They present as cranial swelling that does not cross suture lines. This is in contrast to caput succedaneum, which is a supra-periosteal hematoma that does cross suture lines. Most commonly, cephalohematomas self-resolve without intervention. Complications include calcification of the hematoma with prolonged bony swelling and cranial deformities, infection, and osteomyelitis. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia can occur because of the resorption of extravasated blood products.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Blood under the galea aponeurotica (Choice A) describes a subgaleal hemorrhage, which occurs secondary to trauma sustained during vaginal or assisted vaginal deliveries. It occurs because of shearing of the emissary veins that connect the scalp to the dural sinuses, and it carries the potential for significant hemorrhage. It presents with a diffuse swelling of the head that continues to worsen after delivery, tachycardia, and pallor. Cerebrospinal fluid under the galea aponeurotica (Choice C) and under the periosteum of the parietal bone (Choice D) could occur following skull fractures, which are rare complications of uncomplicated and assisted vaginal deliveries. These can present with leptomeningeal cysts. Contusion of the scalp (Choice E) is commonly to the result of injury to the head, which causes damage to small blood vessels. It would present as ecchymosis, rather than a fluctuant swelling over the parietal area. Educational Objective: Cephalohematomas are traumatic subperiosteal hematomas that can occur as complications of uncomplicated or assisted vaginal deliveries. They result in fluctuant swelling that does not cross suture lines.

questionStem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of lethargy. There is no history of trauma , and she has not had fever, diarrhea , or vomiting . She was born at 27 weeks' gestation , and required 2 months of ventilatory support and a 2-week course of dexamethasone therapy for respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn and bronchopulmonary dysplasia . She had an umbilical arterial and venous catheter in place during the first 2 weeks of life. Her temperature is 36. 7°C (98.1 °F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 110/85 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation . Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities . Doppler ultrasonography shows renal artery thrombosis . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's hypertension?
correctExplanation: Renal artery thrombosis is a rare complication of umbilical artery catheterization that can present up to several weeks after the catheter has been removed. Other risk factors include sepsis, volume depletion, and a patent ductus arteriosus. Occlusion of the renal artery by the thrombus results in decreased afferent blood flow to the affected kidney and increased renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus. The overstimulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system results in secondary hypertension. Treatment of renal artery thrombosis includes systemic anticoagulation and volume resuscitation. Unilateral nephrectomy may be required in refractory hypertension.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Choice A) can result in pulmonary hypertension as a result of chronic hypoxia and vascular remodeling, which commonly occurs in adults. It would be unlikely in a 3-month-old patient. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice B), also called pseudotumor cerebri, is a condition of increased intracranial pressure without an identifiable cause. It most commonly presents in younger female patients; risk factors include obesity, and use of vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol. It is usually associated with a holocephalic headache and blurry vision. Prematurity (Choice D) is a risk factor for surfactant deficiency and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Steroid therapy is indicated to promote surfactant production. Prolonged use of corticosteroids (Choice E) can result in hypertension as a result of the increased fluid retention from mineralocorticoid effects on the kidneys. Dexamethasone is a potent glucocorticoid that has minimal mineralocorticoid effects and is unlikely to produce significant hypertension, especially weeks after exposure. Educational Objective: Impaired perfusion to one or both of the kidneys is a potential cause of secondary hypertension. Renal artery thrombosis is a rare disorder associated with umbilical artery catheterization. Occlusion of the renal artery by the thrombus results in decreased afferent blood flow to the affected kidney and increased renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of vomiting for 20 hours and lethargy for 4 hours . Earlier that day, she fell and struck the side of her head on a coffee table while demonstrating a new dance step ; she did not lose consciousness at that time . Vomiting began approximately 4 hours after she hit her head . On arrival , she is sleepy but oriented . Her pulse is 76/min , and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. There is a 4-cm round soft area of swelling over the left parietal bone . Optic fundi are difficult to examine , but there are no obvious hemorrhages . A CT scan shows a lens-shaped extracerebral density underlying the parietal swelling . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Epidural hematomas are most commonly associated with trauma to the middle meningeal artery that causes accumulation of blood between the dura and the skull, which is bound by dural sutures. They classically present following head trauma with initial loss of consciousness followed by a brief period of lucidity before later developing altered mental status, headache, emesis, lethargy, and signs of cerebral compression. Physical examination may disclose lateralizing signs, such as hemiparesis, or signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as papilledema. Prompt diagnosis is critical, and initial evaluation should include a noncontrast head CT scan, which will show a lens-shaped hyperdense lesion with adjacent cerebral compression and possible midline shift. Definitive management is surgical evacuation, and occasionally, hyperosmolar therapy if there is impending cerebral herniation.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Cerebral contusions (Choice A) are seen in acceleration or deceleration injuries, particularly in the basal frontal and temporal areas. Symptoms are broad and include headache, altered mental status, loss of consciousness, emesis, or seizure. Imaging will show multiple small, diffuse hyperdense lesions. Concussions (Choice B) are mild forms of traumatic brain injury. They commonly present with confusion and amnesia, headache, and dizziness. MRI of the brain typically shows no abnormalities. Diffuse axonal injury (Choice C) is a severe form of traumatic brain injury that presents immediately after injury with profoundly altered mental status or coma caused by shearing of white matter tracts. Neuroimaging will show small, hyperdense lesions in the white matter, rather than a lens-shaped lesion. lntracerebral hematoma (Choice E) presents acutely with headache, altered mental status, hemiplegia, vision changes, aphasia, or coma depending on the area affected. It would be visualized as a hyperdensity within the parenchyma, rather than near the cranial bones. Shaken baby syndrome (Choice F) typically presents with lethargy or altered mental status, seizures, and apnea. Physical examination may disclose injuries that are inconsistent with the history as well as retinal hemorrhages. Neuroimaging will typically show cerebral contusions from an acceleration or deceleration injury, along with potential subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhages. Subdural hematoma (Choice G) commonly presents following trauma with a collection of blood beneath the dura as a result of shearing of the bridging veins. They are crescent-shaped on CT scan, rather than lens­ shaped. Educational Objective: Epidural hematomas present following trauma with initial loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval prior to developing altered mental status, headache, emesis, lethargy, and signs of cerebral compression. A non-contrast head CT scan will show an extracerebral lens-shaped hyperdense lesion bound by suture lines.

questionStem: A 3-month-old infant is inactive and slow in feeding and has constipation . Her serum thyroxine (T 4) concentration is decreased and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is increased . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: Thyroid dysgenesis involves the underdevelopment or complete absence of thyroid tissue. It is commonly caused by a mutation in PAXB, encoding a paired box transcription factor. Paired box transcription factors are crucial for the proper embryologic development of tissues throughout the body, and mutations in paired box genes cause a variety of diseases characterized by improper tissue development, such as Waardenburg syndrome, aniridia, ocular coloboma, optic nerve hypoplasia, oligodontia, and kidney hypoplasia. Thyroid dysgenesis presents in infancy with symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as lethargy, poor feeding, and constipation. Characteristically, serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentrations are increased, and serum concentrations of thyroid hormone are decreased or absent.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Deficiency in T 4-binding globulin (Choice A) is a rare, inherited condition that is usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on thyroid laboratory studies. It is not a common cause of symptomatic hypothyroidism. Hypopituitarism (Choice B) may cause secondary hypothyroidism because of the inadequate production of TSH. TSH concentrations would be decreased, which is not consistent with this patient's laboratory findings. Lymphocytic thyroiditis (Choice C), also known as Hashimoto disease, is the most common form of thyroiditis and presents with signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism. Hashimoto disease most commonly affects middle aged women, although teens and rarely children can be affected. During infancy, Hashimoto disease is rare, and alternate diagnoses such as thyroid dysgenesis are more likely. Unresponsiveness to thyroid hormone (Choice E) is a rare disorder characterized by diffuse peripheral tissue unresponsiveness to binding of the thyroid hormone receptor by thyroid hormone. It may present with goiter and symptoms of hypothyroidism. Serum concentrations of T 4 are characteristically increased in order to overcome the unresponsiveness of the peripheral tissues. Educational Objective: Thyroid dysgenesis involves the underdevelopment or complete absence of thyroid tissue. Thyroid dysgenesis presents in infancy with symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as lethargy, poor feeding, and constipation. Characteristically, serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentrations are increased, and serum concentrations of thyroid hormone are decreased or absent.

questionStem: A previously healthy 16-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of decreased appetite , poor weight gain, and intermittent diarrhea over the past 3 months . He has vomited once during this period . He has not had fever, and his activity level has been normal. At the age of 12 months, he was at the 50th percentile for length and weight. He is now at the 50th percentile for length and 20th percentile for weight. Examination shows mild abdominal distention . Test of the stool is positive for Giardia Jamblia and negative for occult blood . Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this child's failure to thrive?

choices.E: Utilization of nutrients by the parasite

correctExplanation: Giardia Jamblia is a flagellated, parasitic organism that causes giardiasis. Giardiasis is usually acquired through the ingestion of cysts in contaminated water, which then mature into trophozoites in the small bowel. Parasitic overgrowth of the small bowel leads to the intestinal malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates. Giardiasis presents with persistent diarrhea that is foul-smelling and fatty, as well as abdominal pain, bloating, cramping, and weight loss. Children and infants are more likely than adults to present with dehydration and may experience failure to thrive as a result of malnutrition secondary to malabsorption. Diagnosis is made with stool culture, microscopy, or stool antigen testing. Light microscopy shows a flagellated, pear-shaped trophozoite with two large, central nuclei, and a medial axostyle. Metronidazole is the first line treatment.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hypermetabolic state (Choice A) can occur as a consequence of hyperthyroidism. Infection with G. Jamblia does not cause perturbations in thyroid function. Inherited disaccharidase deficiency (Choice B) underlies lactose intolerance. Infection with G. Jamblia does not cause lactose intolerance. Overgrowth of saprophytic organisms (Choice D) is not consistent with the presence of G. Jamblia. Saprophytic organisms derive their energy from the digestion of decaying organic matter and include molds and fungi. G. Jamblia is neither a fungus nor a saprophytic organism. Utilization of nutrients by the parasite (Choice E) does not underlie the mechanism of diarrhea and failure to thrive caused by giardiasis. While G. Jamblia does survive in the human small bowel as a parasite and does utilize nutrients found there, small bowel parasitic overgrowth leading to intestinal malabsorption is the underlying cause of subsequent diarrhea and failure to thrive. Educational Objective: Giardia Jamblia is a flagellated, parasitic organism that causes giardiasis. It presents with persistent diarrhea that is foul-smelling and fatty, as well as abdominal pain, bloating, cramping, and weight loss as a result of small bowel parasitic overgrowth and the resultant malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates.

questionStem: Two weeks after a camping trip in New England , a 5-year-old boy develops a 3-cm, red, circular lesion with a clear center, lymphadenopathy , conjunctivitis , myalgia , and nausea . Antibodies to Proteus vulgaris Ox-19 are negative . Which of the following is the most likely causal agent?
correctExplanation: Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is endemic in the Northeastern United States and commonly transmitted by the lxodes scapularis tick. In its early stages, it causes erythema chronicum migrans, which is an expanding rash that may have a central ring-like clearing. It can also be associated with a flu-like illness. Lyme disease can be treated with amoxicillin or doxycycline in the early stages, with amoxicillin preferred in pediatric patients. Doxycycline, which acts by preventing the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to ribosomes has adverse effects that include gastrointestinal distress, photosensitivity, and in children, discoloration of teeth and inhibition of bone growth, which makes it contraindicated in pregnancy and children under the age of 8 years. Later stages of Lyme disease can be characterized by carditis, atrioventricular heart block, facial nerve palsy (which may be bilateral), migratory arthralgias, and if left untreated, encephalopathy and chronic arthritis. Later stages of Lyme disease that affect the heart or central nervous system are generally treated with parenteral ceftriaxone. Other spirochetes include Leptospira and Treponema. Infection with Leptospira interrogans, found in water contaminated with animal urine, causes leptospirosis. Leptospirosis is characterized by flu-like symptoms, myalgias, jaundice, and photophobia with conjunctiva! injection. Treponema pallidum is the organism responsible for causing syphilis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bacterial infections (Choice A) can cause a wide variety of infections, including impetigo and cellulitis ( Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes), as well as folliculitis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa or S. aureus). However, Lyme disease is more characteristic of a circular lesion with central clearing, associated with lymphadenopathy and myalgias. Fungal infections (Choice B) of the skin include tinea corporis, tinea capitis, and tinea pedis, which are all dermatophyte infections. Tinea corporis, or ringworm, presents with a pruritic circular lesion with a central area of clearing. However, the lesion is usually scaly and not associated with systemic findings. Rickettsia infections (Choice C) include Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhus. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is transmitted by a tick but presents with a vasculitic rash that affects the palms and soles. Typhus, on the other hand, starts with a generalized rash on the trunk that spreads outward and spares the palms and soles. Neither causes a singular, circular lesion. Viral infections (Choice E) of the skin include varicella zoster virus and herpes simplex virus. Both present with a vesicular rash, rather than a single lesion with central clearing. Educational Objective: Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and characteristically causes erythema chronicum migrans, an expanding rash that may have a central ring­ like clearing. It is treated with doxycycline or amoxicillin in the early stages, with amoxicillin preferred in pediatric patients. Ceftriaxone is indicated for late stage or disseminated cases.

questionStem: A 2-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 30-minute history of her chest "fluttering ." Thirty minutes ago, she vomited after breast-feeding . She was born at 40 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. She weighed 3402 g (7 lb 8 oz) at birth. On arrival , she is awake and appears alert. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is too rapid to count , respirations are 48/min , and blood pressure is 74/48 mm Hg. The extremities are pink and warm ; capillary refill time is less than 2 seconds . The lungs are clear to auscultation . No murmurs are heard on cardiac examination . An ECG shows a regular heart rate of 240/min , a ORS complex duration of 0.05 seconds , and no discernible P waves . Application of an ice bag to the face for 5 seconds does not change the heart rate . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) commonly occurs in children and infants and is characterized by paroxysmal episodes of rapid, narrow-complex tachycardia. SVT is often idiopathic and paroxysmal but may occur secondary to accessory pathways in some children with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Diagnosis is made by ECG, although some children may require cardiac monitoring in order to capture a paroxysmal event. AV nodal blockade with adenosine is the first line treatment for narrow complex SVT. Adenosine is a purine analogue that acts on the adenosine receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor that signals through adenylate cyclase. In the AV node, binding of the adenosine Arreceptor leads to cellular hyperpolarization and reduced transmission of supraventricular action potentials. If adenosine fails, synchronized cardioversion may be attempted. Children who are old enough may be trained to use vagal maneuvers in order to naturally induce AV nodal blockade. A similar vagal maneuver may be attempted by placing an ice bag over the eyes and face for approximately 30 seconds.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Administration of digoxin {Choice B) is useful in the management of congestive heart failure and of atrial fibrillation and flutter. It is not used in the treatment of SVT. Administration of procainamide {Choice C), a sodium channel blocker, may be useful in achieving chemical cardioversion in atrial fibrillation, but is not a first line agent for the treatment of SVT when narrow complex. It is commonly used in arrhythmia management in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, especially in cases of antidromic reentrant tachycardia. Administration of verapamil {Choice D), a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is useful for control of SVT but is not a first-line agent for aborting the acute arrhythmia. It is also useful for the management of cluster headache. Catheter ablation {Choice E) is useful for the treatment of accessory pathways in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. While Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome may be diagnosed in infancy, paroxysmal SVT is more common. Unsynchronized cardioversion {Choice F) delivers an electrical shock at any point within the cardiac cycle. This method is reserved for pulseless ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. In patients with SVT who fail treatment with adenosine, synchronized cardioversion is preferred. Educational Objective: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) commonly occurs in children and infants and is characterized by paroxysmal episodes of rapid, narrow-complex tachycardia. AV nodal blockade with adenosine is the first-line treatment. In the AV node, binding the adenosine Arreceptor leads to cellular hyperpolarization and reduced transmission of supraventricular action potentials.

questionStem: An otherwise asymptomatic 4-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing jaundice for 1 week . He was born at term following a prolonged labor. One day after birth, he received phototherapy for jaundice and was discharged on the third day. He is exclusively breast-fed . Examination shows no abnormalities except for jaundice . Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dl with normal red cell morphology , and a total serum bilirubin concentration of 12 mg/dl with a direct component of 8 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's jaundice ?

choices.C: Decreased hepatic Y and Z protein concentrations

correctExplanation: Neonatal jaundice with a preponderance of conjugated bilirubin, as indicated by an increased direct bilirubin, is suggestive of biliary atresia. Biliary atresia is caused by the abnormal underdevelopment of the extrahepatic biliary system. Affected infants are able to conjugate bilirubin normally in the liver but are unable to excrete bile into the gastrointestinal lumen. Affected infants present with worsening jaundice caused by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, along with pale stool, dark urine, poor weight gain, and, in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and therefore does not cause kernicterus. Treatment includes surgical portoenterostomy to allow bile to be excreted or a liver transplant.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreased hepatic glucuronosyltransferase activity (Choice B) underlies the pathogenesis of Gilbert syndrome and Crigler-Najjar syndrome. Both of these diseases are characterized by defective hepatic conjugation of bilirubin. Accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin is identified by an increased serum concentration of indirect bilirubin. Decreased hepatic Y and Z protein concentrations (Choice C) would interfere with hepatic bilirubin conjugation. These two proteins are involved in the cytosolic binding of bilirubin in hepatocytes and allow for the transport of bilirubin to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum for metabolic processing. Decreased serum bilirubin uptake (Choice D) would occur in hypoalbuminemia. Circulating serum bilirubin is unconjugated and water insoluble. Normal transport of serum bilirubin to the liver is dependent upon normal concentrations of albumin, to which bilirubin is bound and thereby solubilized. Increased serum bilirubin production (Choice E) is suggestive of hemolytic disease, such as sickle cell disease. lntravascular hemolysis can be identified by increased serum concentrations of indirect, or unconjugated, bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, and decreased serum concentrations of haptoglobin. Educational Objective: Biliary atresia is caused by the abnormal underdevelopment of the extrahepatic biliary system. Affected infants present with worsening jaundice caused by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, along with pale stool, dark urine, poor weight gain, and, in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension.

questionStem: A 4-year-old boy is hospitalized because of fever, shallow breathing , and unresponsiveness for 3 hours. His temperature is 40°C (104°F) , pulse is 160/min, respirations are 60/min , and blood pressure is 60/35 mm Hg. Examination shows purpura over the lower extremities . He is intubated and mechanically ventilated . Blood cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis . Two days later, an x-ray of the chest shows bilateral patchy infiltrates . Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for these findings ?
correctExplanation: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a severe complication associated with numerous causes, including sepsis, aspiration, pneumonia, trauma, and shock. The syndrome results from the effect of cytokines on the pulmonary parenchyma following direct or indirect lung injury. This results in endothelial injury with increased vascular permeability. Exudative fluid extends into the alveolar space, resulting in diffuse alveolar damage and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. ARDS is characterized by respiratory failure with bilateral diffuse interstitial and airspace opacities from underlying diffuse alveolar damage and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Mechanical ventilation is often required in the management of ARDS as a result of hypoxemia and hypoventilation.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Cholinergic hyperactivity (Choice A) may result in cholinergic crisis as a result of excessive stimulation of nicotinic and muscarinic receptors. In the lungs, this results in decreased lung compliance, bronchoconstriction, and increased bronchial secretions. Potential causes include organophosphate toxicity and acetylcholinesterase inhibitor overdose. Enzymatic deficiency (Choice B) is characteristic of arantitrypsin deficiency, which results in host tissue damage from neutrophil elastase in the lungs and liver. Imaging typically shows emphysematous changes in the bilateral lung bases. Mucosal inflammation (Choice D) occurs with direct lung irritation or injury, as in pulmonary infection, chemical pneumonitis, inflammatory lung disease, foreign body aspiration, and malignancy. ARDS is characterized by increased vascular permeability in the alveoli rather than the mucosa. Oxygen toxicity (Choice E) is a complication of mechanical ventilation with high fraction of inspired oxygen. Exposure to high concentrations of oxygen can lead to cell membrane oxidative damage and collapse of alveoli, with extensive pulmonary edema and development of ARDS. This patient who was otherwise healthy prior to his infection without pulmonary involvement likely has a low fraction of inspired oxygen, and ARDS resulting from sepsis and increased vascular permeability is more likely than oxygen toxicity. Surfactant deficiency (Choice F) is the underlying pathophysiology of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome caused by alveolar collapse in inadequate surfactant production. Surfactant deficiency may also result from drowning injury or aspiration which dilutes the alveolar concentration of surfactant. Educational Objective: Acute respiratory distress syndrome is a life-threatening inflammatory disorder characterized by increased pulmonary vascular permeability and diffuse pulmonary edema with a proteinaceous exudate. It is associated with numerous causes, especially sepsis, aspiration, pneumonia, trauma, and shock.

questionStem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a well-child examination . She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. A grade 2/6, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur with a musical quality is heard best at the lower left sternal border with no radiation . S2 is normal. Precordial activity and peripheral pulses are normal. There were no previous notations of a murmur in her medical records . An ECG shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance that this is a benign murmu

correctExplanation: A Still murmur is a benign, asymptomatic murmur heard in children. It is a systolic, musical, grade 1 to 2 murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border. It is typically louder when the patient is supine than when the patient is sitting. It most commonly self-resolves by adolescence. Pathologic murmurs are more frequently heard in infants under one year of age, caused by abnormalities such as valve disorders or shunt lesions, whereas murmurs heard after one year of age are more frequently benign, although they can be caused by valve stenosis, regurgitation, or atrial septal defects. Pathologic murmurs also present with related symptoms, such as dyspnea, diaphoresis, or failure to thrive. Further evaluation is recommended for murmurs that are grade 3 or greater in intensity, diastolic, at maximal intensity at the left upper sternal border, holosystolic, or have a harsh or blowing quality. It is also recommended for murmurs that are more intense in the upright position. As this patient has a benign Still murmur, reassurance is appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete blood count (CBC) (Choice B) could be used to evaluate for infection or anemia as a cause of the murmur. Endocarditis causes lesions of the heart valves that can present with heart murmurs as well as leukocytosis on CBC, whereas severe anemia can lead to a functional murmur. This patient has a benign murmur; a CBC is not indicated. Chest x-rays (Choice C) can be used in the initial evaluation of cyanotic and non-cyanotic congenital heart disease. For example, tetralogy of Fallo! can present with a systolic ejection murmur heard in the left upper sternal border because of pulmonic stenosis, as well as a boot-shaped heart on chest x-ray. However, a chest x-ray in this patient would show no abnormalities. Echocardiography (Choice D) is used to evaluate the structure and function of the heart. If this patient had a concerning murmur, such as a diastolic grade 4/6 murmur, echocardiography would be the most appropriate next step. However, it plays no role in the evaluation of this benign murmur. Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures (Choice E) is recommended to prevent the development of infective endocarditis for patients with prosthetic heart valves, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, repaired congenital heart disease (with residual shunts, valvular regurgitation, or an occlusion device), or valve regurgitation in a transplanted heart. This patient does not require antibiotic prophylaxis. Educational Objective: A Still murmur is a benign, asymptomatic murmur of childhood that presents with a systolic, grade 1 to 2 murmur with a musical quality best heard at the lower left sternal border.

questionStem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of headache , nausea , and vomiting during football practice . Although practice was held in the evening , the temperature outside was 85°F, and the humidity was 80%. The patient reports that he had been drinking water frequently during practice . He had not eaten since breakfast. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . He is at the 90th percentile for height, weight , and BMI. On arrival, he is alert, responsive , and severely diaphoretic . His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 110/77 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities . Genital and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 3. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Athletes are at increased risk for heat exhaustion as a result of strenuous exercise in hot temperatures and increased humidity. Other risk factors include lack of acclimatization, obesity, dehydration, and poor physical fitness. During exertion, the body is able to dissipate heat by increasing blood flow to skin and producing sweat to facilitate evaporative cooling. However, when ambient temperature is increased and humidity is high, these mechanisms are less effective at dissipating heat, resulting in heat exhaustion. Heat exhaustion is characterized by exercise intolerance, increased core body temperature, and the absence of neurologic disturbances (eg, altered mental status, confusion, or seizure). It is also associated with dehydration, tachycardia, lightheadedness, muscle cramps, and generalized weakness. Neurologic disturbances are associated with a more severe form of exertional heat illness referred to as heat stroke. Management of heat exhaustion involves removing the individual from the heat, removing excess clothing, and initiating cooling measures such as immersion in cool water or evaporative cooling.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute gastroenteritis {Choice A) is a common, typically self-limiting illness in children characterized by nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and mild abdominal discomfort. Although this patient has nausea and vomiting, he does not have diarrhea, and heat exhaustion is more likely. Hypoglycemia {Choice C) can cause confusion, altered mental status, lightheadedness, and syncope. The patient would be at risk for hypoglycemia as a result of exercising after not eating since breakfast. However, healthy individuals are typically able to maintain a stable serum glucose concentration because of hepatic glycogenolysis during periods of exercise and fasting. Hypoglycemia would not cause hyperthermia. Hyponatremic dehydration {Choice D) can occur in subacute or chronic severe vomiting and diarrhea as a result of the loss of electrolytes, including sodium, and water. Dehydration increases the action of antidiuretic hormone, leading to increased free water reabsorption in the collecting tubule and can further contribute to hyponatremia. Malignant hyperthermia {Choice E) is caused by a genetic defect in the ryanodine receptor and presents with muscle rigidity, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and lactic acidosis when a patient is exposed to succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics. Risk factors include family history, being born in the upper Midwest of the United States, and certain musculoskeletal disorders. Dantrolene is the treatment of choice. Educational Objective: Heat exhaustion is characterized by exercise intolerance, increased core body temperature, and the absence of neurologic disturbances. It is associated with dehydration, tachycardia, lightheadedness, muscle cramps, and generalized weakness.

questionStem: A previously healthy 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after being stabbed in the left side of her chest with a pair of scissors . En route to the hospital , intravenous lactated Ringer solution was administered , and administration of oxygen (3 Umin) via face mask was begun . On arrival, she has severe chest pain. She is agitated and diaphoretic and is not oriented to person , place, or time . Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min and labored , and palpable systolic blood pressure is 80 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention bilaterally. The trachea is deviated to the right. Breath sounds are decreased on the left with hyperresonance to percussion . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
correctExplanation: Tension pneumothorax can be a complication of a penetrating thoracic trauma and occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. Increasing amounts of trapped air in the pleural space compresses the lung parenchyma, creating an inability for the lung to expand and causing it to collapse. As the pneumothorax progresses and continues to increase in size, it can result in tracheal or mediastinal deviation away from the affected hemithorax. It can also result in compression of the pulmonary veins and superior vena cava, decreasing venous return to the left and right atria, which manifests with hypotension, jugular venous distension, and obstructive shock. Tension pneumothorax is characterized by absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion caused by increased air in the intrathoracic space displacing normal lung parenchyma. In an unstable patient, air from a tension pneumothorax should be evacuated by an emergent needle decompression followed by a tube thoracostomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chest x-ray (Choice A) would not be the appropriate next step in management of this unstable patient. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and immediate management should involve evacuation of air from the intrapleural space. Insertion of an oropharyngeal airway (Choice B) is indicated during bag-valve mask ventilation of a patient, especially in cases of a tongue obstructing the airway. It is an adjunct that helps open the airway to allow for easier ventilation. Pericardiocentesis (Choice D) is appropriate in cases of pericardia! effusion or tamponade, which typically present following symptoms of pericarditis, or with muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and hypotension if tamponade from any cause is present. Pulsus paradoxus may be disclosed on examination. This patient's jugular venous distension is a result of tension pneumothorax, not pericardia! tamponade. Cricothyroidotomy (Choice E) is a type of invasive airway access. It may be indicated in cases of airway compromise in which endotracheal intubation is unsuccessful. Educational Objective: Tension pneumothorax occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. This leads to an increasing amount of air trapped in the pleural space with subsequent collapse of the lung parenchyma and mass effect on the mediastinum. It is characterized by respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, hypotension, decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance to percussion on physical examination. Management requires emergent needle decompression followed by placement of a chest tube.

questionStem: After undergoing a tonsillectomy , a 2-year-old boy develops seizures in the recovery room. During the 45-minute operation , he received 1 L of 5% dextrose in water. Measurement of which of the following serum concentrations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The patient is likely suffering from acute hyponatremia complicated by seizures after receiving hypotonic fluids for his procedure. Measurement of the sodium concentration will confirm the diagnosis. Sodium is the most prevalent extracellular cation, and maintaining a normal serum concentration is essential for the proper functioning of tissue and movement of water between the intracellular and extracellular spaces. Derangements of sodium concentration are mostly caused by imbalances in water content of the extracellular fluid (as regulated by antidiuretic hormone activity) as opposed to actual changes in total body sodium content. Administration of hypotonic fluids such as 5% dextrose in water dilutes the serum, resulting in osmotic pressure that drives water molecules into the intracellular space. The primary acute symptoms are because of an acute cerebral edema, which can progress to altered mental status, gait disturbances, seizures, coma, and death. Management requires the careful return of sodium to normal serum concentrations.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Creatinine (Choice A) is used as a marker for the glomerular filtration rate. Increased serum creatinine concentrations can indicate acute kidney injury, which can be a complication of surgery as a result of transient hypotension. Administration of intravenous fluids during procedures reduces this risk. Glucose (Choice B) concentrations are likely increased in this patient receiving dextrose. Decreased glucose concentration can present with altered mental status and seizures. In the absence of insulin resistance, temporarily increased glucose concentrations are unlikely to cause symptoms. Potassium (Choice C) concentration is unlikely to be altered in this otherwise healthy patient. Hypo- and hyperkalemia increase the risk for cardiac dysrhythmias. Urea nitrogen (Choice E) concentration may be increased in acute kidney injury or because of increased gut absorption of urea nitrogen products in a gastrointestinal bleed. Increased urea nitrogen concentrations may cause uremic syndrome, which presents with fatigue, nausea, and altered mental status. Educational Objective: Hyponatremia is a potential complication of the administration of hypotonic intravenous fluids. Acute hyponatremia results in cerebral edema caused by the movement of water from the extracellular space to the intracellular space, and it may present with altered mental status, ataxia, seizures, coma, and/or death.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by police because of a 5-hour history of hallucinations , profuse sweating , and intermittent yelling and flailing . He is striking out at those near him and requires leather restraints . His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor, profuse diaphoresis , and recent bruising . Mental status examination shows incoherent speech , episodic screaming, and agitation . He is disoriented to person , place, and time . The most appropriate next step in management is administration of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Phencyclidine (PCP) is an illicit substance that acts on the central nervous system in a variety of ways. It antagonizes NMDA receptors leading to excitatory neurotransmitter release, inhibits reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, and stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors. Acute PCP intoxication can lead to psychosis, bizarre behavior, agitation, aggression, rotatory nystagmus, and ataxia. Patients may be diaphoretic, tachycardic, and hypertensive because of sympathomimetic effects. Chronic PCP use can lead to major depressive disorder, psychotic symptoms, memory loss, and dysarthria. Control of psychomotor agitation is the first step in management of patients with PCP intoxication for the safety of the patient and medical staff. Chemical sedation with benzodiazepines such as intramuscular lorazepam or midazolam can be administered to control symptoms. Once a patient is adequately sedated, further evaluation can be completed to assess for traumatic injuries or complications of PCP intoxication such as rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, hypertension, seizures, encephalopathy, or a comatose state.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intramuscular naloxone (Choice B) is indicated for cases of opioid overdose. Opioid overdoses are characterized by respiratory depression presenting as a decreased respiratory rate, apnea, and hypoxia. This patient is severely agitated, making PCP intoxication more likely. Intravenous 50% dextrose (Choice C) is indicated in hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia can cause confusion, altered mental status, lightheadedness, and syncope. Hypoglycemia would be unlikely to cause hypertension and psychomotor agitation as seen in this patient. Intravenous flumazenil (Choice D) is indicated for benzodiazepine overdose. It is a competitive inhibitor of the GABA receptor at the benzodiazepine binding site. Benzodiazepine overdose is characterized by sedation and potential respiratory depression, not psychomotor agitation as seen in this patient. Intravenous 5% glucose and 0.9% saline (Choice E) are typically administered as maintenance fluids in patients who are unable to tolerate oral nutrition or for patients who are fasting prior to a surgical procedure. It would not help in sedating this patient. Educational Objective: Acute PCP intoxication can lead to psychosis, bizarre behavior, agitation, aggression, rotatory nystagmus, and ataxia. Control of psychomotor agitation is the first step in management of patients with PCP intoxication for the safety of the patient and medical staff. Chemical sedation with benzodiazepines such as intramuscular lorazepam or midazolam can be administered to control symptoms.

questionStem: An asymptomatic 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a health maintenance examination . He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . His parents both have essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia . He has an active lifestyle and plays several sports . He consumes a wide variety of foods, including meat, fruit, and vegetables , and drinks two to three glasses each of whole milk and fruit juice daily. He is currently at the 90th percentile for height and above the 97th percentile for weight and BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate dietary recommendation at this time?

choices.B: Begin dietary supplementation with a multivitamin
choices.D: Decrease his intake of milk and fruit juice
choices.E: Increase his intake of fruit and vegetables

correctExplanation: This 10-year-old boy displays signs concerning for obesity given his BMI over the 971h percentile. Pediatric obesity causes health consequences in nearly every organ system including cardiovascular (hypertension, dyslipidemia), endocrine (diabetes mellitus, hyperandrogenism, early menarche), gastrointestinal (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease), musculoskeletal (slipped capital femoral epiphysis), and pulmonary (obesity hypoventilation syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea). This patient is at further increased risk given his family history of hypertension and dyslipidemia. The first step in weight management in this patient is to decrease his caloric intake. His dietary history discloses that he is drinking an excessive amount of highly caloric beverages including whole milk and fruit juice. While milk contains beneficial nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D, whole milk contains approximately 100 calories per 8 oz serving. In contrast, fruit juice has little nutritional value and also contains approximately 100 calories per 8 oz serving. This simple dietary intervention is the most appropriate first step in managing this patient's weight.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Avoid low-fat diets (Choice A) will encourage continued weight gain in this patient rather than help to decrease his weight. By simply decreasing whole milk and fruit juice intake, this patient may not need to pursue any specific diet. There is no evidence that this patient does not have adequate vitamins and minerals in his diet, so there is not an indication to begin dietary supplementation with a multivitamin (Choice B). Furthermore, beginning a multivitamin would not affect the patient's weight, which is the primary concern in this otherwise well child. Continuing his current diet (Choice C) will continue to perpetuate weight gain. It will also promote eating habits which will impact his adolescent and adult years. By improving his eating habits, he will be better prepared to manage his weight in the future. While increasing his intake of fruits and vegetables (Choice E) would be a healthy dietary intervention, it will not improve his weight. However, replacing high calorie, processed snacks with fruits and vegetables is another healthy habit to encourage in children and adolescents. Educational Objective: Childhood and adolescent obesity is becoming increasingly present in resource-rich countries. Obesity in this age group is associated with numerous health detriments. Patients and their parents should be taught healthy eating habits early in life.

questionStem: A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of intermittent fever. During the past 3 days , he has had decreased activity and joint pain. Yesterday he developed a red rash on his chest. He attends day care. He appears pale and is not in acute distress . His temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 24/min . Examination shows a petechial rash over the chest. The conjunctivae are pale. There is diffuse adenopathy in the cervical chain. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard . The spleen is palpated 1 cm below the left costal margin . There is no swelling or redness of the joints . Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 6.4 g/dL, leukocyte count of 50,000/mm 3, and platelet count of 1 0,000/mm 3.

choices.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia G) Lead poisoning
choices.B: Anemia of chronic disease H) Red blood cell aplasia (acquired)

choices.E: Hemolytic uremic syndrome K) Uremia of chronic renal failure

correctExplanation: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia and is likely the result of diffuse bone marrow infiltration by malignant blast cells with subsequent displacement of normal erythroid progenitor cells. The diagnosis of leukemia is supported by the presence of fever, petechial rash, diffuse adenopathy, splenomegaly, and leukocytosis to 50,000/mm 3• Evaluation of the peripheral blood smear would most likely show malignant circulating blasts of the lymphoid lineage. B-lymphocyte malignancies are more common than T-lymphocyte malignancies, and evaluation with flow cytometry is necessary to determine the specific type of malignant cell, followed by mutational analyses. Treatment typically entails chemotherapy and many patients with ALL will enter remission. Bone marrow transplant can be curative in many cases.
incorrectExplanation: Anemia of chronic disease (Choice B) is a common finding in autoimmune and inflammatory disease, chronic infections, and malignancy. Increased hepcidin concentrations decrease iron absorption and increase iron storage in the reticuloendothelial system (RES), which prevents the use of iron by erythrocyte precursors, thereby resulting in anemia. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Choice C) results from the binding of an autoantibody to RBC surface antigens, leading to removal by the RES or to intravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis is made by a positive antiglobulin (Coombs) test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, low haptoglobin, and the presence of spherocytes and reticulocytes on the peripheral smear. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (Choice D) results in oxidative stress and hemolysis upon exposure to certain medications such as sulfa medications. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Choice E) is classically associated with infection from Escherichia coli O157:H7, a Gram-negative rod. It often presents in children with bloody diarrhea, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. Hereditary spherocytosis (Choice F) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins. Peripheral smear shows spherocytes. Definitive treatment is with splenectomy. Lead poisoning (Choice G) inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and ~-ALA dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. Clinical manifestations of lead poisoning include encephalopathy, cognitive dysfunction, peripheral nephropathy, hearing loss, renal tubular dysfunction, interstitial nephritis, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, and anemia. Red blood cell aplasia (acquired) (Choice H) is often an autoimmune process that results in the destruction of erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow leading to anemia with a low reticulocyte count. All other cell lines are unaffected.

questionStem: A 7-year-old girl with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis is brought to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive fatigue . She has had occasional fever and swelling and pain of the knees during the past month . She appears ill. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102 °F), pulse is 104/min , and respirations are 20/min . Examination shows pale conjunctivae . The spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin . The right knee is warm , erythematous , and mildly swollen ; range of motion is limited . Laboratory studies show :

choices.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia G) Lead poisoning
choices.B: Anemia of chronic disease H) Red blood cell aplasia (acquired)
choices.C: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia I) Sickle cell disease
choices.E: Hemolytic uremic syndrome K) Uremia of chronic renal failure

correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Mean corpuscular volume Leukocyte count Reticulocyte count Platelet count 9.5 g/dL 75 µm 3 11 ,000/mm 3 0.5% 400 ,000/mm 3 This patient with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (ie, juvenile idiopathic arthritis) with fevers, fatigue, right knee effusion, and splenomegaly most likely has anemia of chronic disease (ACD). ACD is found in many autoimmune, infectious, and malignant disease states. Chronic inflammation results in increased hepcidin production, which consequently leads to a decreased responsiveness of the bone marrow to erythropoietin and retention of iron within the reticuloendothelial system (RES). This confluence offactors leads to a state of functional iron deficiency despite adequate iron stores. Patients present with either normocytic (early) or microcytic (late) anemia and reduced numbers of reticulocytes, indicating inadequate bone marrow response to anemia. Other laboratory findings include a normal to slightly high ferritin concentration with decreased serum iron concentration and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC).
incorrectExplanation: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Choice A) is a common pediatric malignancy of B or T lymphocytes that may present with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, with circulating leukemic blasts on peripheral blood smear. The mechanism of anemia in this disease is secondary to bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells with obliteration of erythroid precursors. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Choice C) results from the binding of an autoantibody to RBC surface antigens, leading to removal via the RES or to intravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis is made by a positive Coombs test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, decreased haptoglobin, and the presence of spherocytes and reticulocytes on the peripheral smear. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (Choice D) results in oxidative stress and hemolysis upon exposure to certain medications such as sulfa medications. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Choice E) is classically associated with infection from Escherichia coli O157:H?, a Gram-negative rod. It often presents in children with bloody diarrhea, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Hereditary spherocytosis (Choice F) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins. Peripheral smear shows spherocytes. Definitive treatment is with splenectomy. Lead poisoning (Choice G) inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and ~-ALA dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. Clinical manifestations of lead poisoning include encephalopathy, cognitive dysfunction, peripheral nephropathy, hearing loss, renal tubular dysfunction, interstitial nephritis, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, and anemia.

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of lower abdominal cramps and intermittent pain in her knees and hips for 6 weeks . The cramps are relieved by bowel movements . During this period , she has had 6 to 10 urgent, bloody bowel movements daily. Examination shows a swollen , mildly tender left knee joint. Her hemoglobin concentration is 14.5 g/dl , leukocyte count is 16,000/mm 3, and platelet count is 790,000/mm 3. Analysis of knee joint aspirate shows straw-colored , slightly turbid fluid with a leukocyte count of 2000/mm 3 (40% segmented neutrophils) . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ulcerative colitis is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa and submucosa, typically beginning in the rectum and advancing proximally in a continuous distribution. Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus. Imaging typically demonstrates loss of haustral markings. Diagnosis of ulcerative colitis is by colonoscopy and biopsy, which demonstrates characteristic crypt abscesses. Potential complications of ulcerative colitis are fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, and perforation. Inflammatory bowel disease can also be associated with extraintestinal manifestations including uveitis, arthritis, aphthous stomatitis, and pyoderma gangrenosum. Treatment includes immunomodulators, biologics, and steroids, although total colectomy is generally curative and would eliminate the patient's risk for colorectal carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adenovirus gastroenteritis (Choice A) is a cause of self-limited viral gastroenteritis with acute nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea. It would be unlikely to cause bloody diarrhea and 6 weeks of symptoms. Chronic nonspecific diarrhea of childhood (Choice B) is an idiopathic condition characterized by diarrhea in otherwise healthy children. It does not cause weight loss, abdominal pain, or bloody stools. Giardiasis (Choice C) presents with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea, and bloating, typically in campers who ingest cysts from freshwater. It does not typically cause bloody stools. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Choice D) is a small-vessel vasculitis that occurs in children and typically presents with gravity-dependent purpura (eg, buttocks, legs, and feet), arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain (eg, intussusception). Pseudomembranous colitis (Choice E) is caused by C/ostridium difficile, which produces toxins that result in dysfunction of the brush border and a subsequent secretory diarrhea. C. difficile infections are associated with the presence of pseudomembranes that appear as patchy regions of white mucosa on colonoscopy. C. difficile infection is an opportunistic and often hospital-acquired infection that commonly occurs after the use of antibiotics, especially ampicillin and clindamycin, as a result of the loss of native colonic microbiota. Educational Objective: Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa and submucosa. Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus.

questionStem: A previously healthy 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressively worsening headaches and difficulty walking over the past 6 weeks . Examination shows bilateral papilledema , right abducens palsy, and gait ataxia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The peak incidence is between ages 5 and 9 years of age, and they are frequently located in the cerebellum. The position of a medulloblastoma in the cerebellum typically leads to occlusion of ventricular drainage, which causes increases in intracranial pressure. Thus, patients typically present with headaches or nausea (from increased intracranial pressure), as well as gait ataxia or incoordination (caused by cerebellar disruption), as in this patient. Physical examination will often demonstrate nystagmus, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, cranial nerve palsies, and papilledema. Diagnosis is made with MRI and biopsy, with the specimen for the latter most commonly taken during surgical resection. Lumbar punctures are also performed to evaluate for metastatic spread through the cerebrospinal fluid and spinal leptomeninges. In addition to surgery, treatment includes radiation and chemotherapy. Complications include neurologic abnormalities, such as developmental delay and hearing loss, and endocrine abnormalities.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acoustic neuroma (Choice A) is a benign tumor of Schwann cells that arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve. It presents with ipsilateral hearing loss and vertigo, as well as ipsilateral dysmetria if compressing the cerebral peduncles. This patient does not have hearing loss. Dandy-Walker syndrome (Choice B) is a condition in which the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle are malformed, resulting in cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle and posterior fossa with consequent hydrocephalus. It presents early in life with developmental delay, hydrocephalus, and cerebellar or cranial nerve dysfunction. It would be less likely in this previously healthy 7-year-old. Optic nerve glioma (Choice D) is a neoplasm of the optic nerve that is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, although it can occur independently. It is most frequently an astrocytoma that occurs in childhood. It presents with a gradual onset of proptosis, vision loss, and less frequently, hydrocephalus and endocrinopathies because of spread. This patient has had relatively acute onset of symptoms of ataxia and cranial nerve palsies without evidence of vision loss. Pinealoma (Choice E) classically presents with a paralysis of upward gaze, diplopia, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. While this patient does have increased intracranial pressure and right abducens palsy, he does not have a paralysis of upward gaze. Educational Objective: Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor in children, often presenting in patients aged five to nine years with signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, headache, nausea, vomiting) and gait ataxia or incoordination. Treatment requires surgical resection, radiation, and chemotherapy.

questionStem: A previously healthy 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of right scrotal pain and swelling for 3 hours. There is no history of trauma . He was sexually active 3 months ago , and he did not use a condom . Examination shows tenderness and edema in the region of the right testicle . The cremasteric reflex is absent on the right side. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
