correctExplanation: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The resultant twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein, results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow to the testis. Patients typically present with acute, severe testicular pain with diffuse tenderness and swelling. Patients may also exhibit nausea, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain. There is typically a negative cremasteric reflex with a high-riding, transverse lie of the testicle on physical examination. If not properly and expeditiously managed with surgical detorsion and orchiopexy, testicular torsion can result in testicular infarction as well as infertility.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Leukemic infiltration of the testis (Choice A) is seen in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Because of the blood-testis barrier, chemotherapy is less able to reach the testis. Testicular leukemia presents as painless testicular enlargement. Malignant infiltration of the testis (Choice B) can occur in testicular tumors such as seminoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, or yolk sac tumor. Presentation is variable depending on the type of tumor. Seminoma is the most common testicular tumor and presents as painless testicular enlargement. Persistent patency of the processus vaginalis (Choice C) can lead to the formation of a hydrocele if filled by peritoneal fluid, or hematocele if complicated by blood accumulation. It also increases the risk for an indirect inguinal hernia. Persistent patency of the urachus (Choice D) contributes to a persistent connection between the bladder and the umbilicus. Patients with a patent urachus can present with clear urine leaking out of the umbilicus. It can also be asymptomatic or potentially complicated by infection. Educational Objective: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The resultant twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein, results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow.

questionStem: A healthy 9-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a well-child examination . Her parents are concerned that she is not gaining enough weight. She is breast-feeding six times daily and taking small amounts of baby food from a spoon. She is at the 5th percentile for weight and 25th percentile for length and head circumference . Review of the growth chart shows that this growth pattern has been consistent since birth. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance that this growth i:>attern is within normal limits
choices.B: Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food
choices.D: Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk

correctExplanation: Growth charts show the percentile curves of body measurements such as head circumference, body weight, and length for children. They are used to evaluate for normal growth, short stature, growth delay, failure to thrive, nutritional deficiencies, malabsorption, endocrinopathy, and other disorders. Clinicians use the growth chart provided by the World Health Organization (WHO), which is an international standard for infant growth. For infants less than 2 years of age, infants are classified as low weight or short stature if they are less than 2nd percentile for weight or length, respectively. This patient is the 5th percentile for weight, which, while low, is not yet of concern. In addition, her growth pattern has been consistent since birth. Further assessment to investigate growth or nutritional problems should be performed if infants are less than the 2nd percentile or if there are major changes in growth pattern.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food (Choice B) would not be an appropriate recommendation, as the patient's weight and length are within normal limits on the growth chart. This may be an appropriate recommendation if the patient's weight was less than the 2nd percentile and the reason for growth delay was inadequate caloric intake. Replacing breast-feeding with soy-based formula (Choice C) would not be appropriate. Breastfeeding is a standard source of nutrition for the growth and healthy development of infants. Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk (Choice D) would be harmful to the infant. Early introduction of whole cow's milk prior to one year of age has been associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus, increased risk for developing cow's milk allergy, constipation, and iron deficiency anemia. Educational Objective: Growth charts show the percentile curves of body measurements such as head circumference, body weight, and length for children. Patients less than 2 years of age are classified as low weight or short stature if they are less than the 2nd percentile for weight or length, respectively.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 6-month history of increasingly severe pain with menses . Her mother reports that during this time , her daughter has missed 2 days of school during each menstrual period because of severe pelvic cramps associated with vomiting . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 4 to 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 7 days ago . She currently takes acetaminophen , which provides minimal relief of her symptoms . She has had three lifetime sexual partners , and they use condoms inconsistently . The patient is an honor roll student despite frequent absences from school. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows a tender, normal-sized uterus and no masses . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy females and occurs in the absence of secondary causes, such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis, or uterine fibroids. Symptoms often begin during adolescence and commonly interfere with quality of life and with essential activities such as school or work. Patients describe crampy lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses, which persists for several days, along with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Endometrial sloughing is accompanied by the production of prostaglandins, which stimulate painful uterine contractions. Patients are typically treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, thereby limiting prostaglandin synthesis, or with oral hormonal contraceptives.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A pregnancy test (Choice A) can be used to evaluate for pregnancy, particularly ectopic pregnancy in the setting of severe abdominal pain. However, this patient's most recent period was 7 days ago, making pregnancy unlikely. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice B) can be used to evaluate for structural abnormalities of the uterus or adnexa, such as fibroids or ovarian cysts that can cause recurrent abdominopelvic pain. However, there was no evidence of structural abnormalities during this patient's pelvic examination. Narcotic therapy (Choice C) carries a high risk for physical dependence and opioid use disorder. It would be inappropriate to start narcotic therapy for pain control in this patient before trying other options, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy. Selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor therapy (Choice E) is used in the treatment of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. It does not play a role in the management of primary dysmenorrhea. Educational Objective: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy females and occurs in the absence of secondary causes. Symptoms include crampy lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses and persists for several days, as well as fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

questionStem: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician 2 months after his parents noticed that he seemed to be ignoring them. On questioning , they note that he does not appear to be startled by loud noises. Growth and development have been otherwise normal. He was born at term to a 28-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1. His mother's blood group is A, Rh-negative , and his blood group is A, Rh-positive . He had a serum total bilirubin concentration of 25 mg/dL at the age of 2 days and received phototherapy for 2 days. He continued to be mildly jaundiced until the age of 1 month. Serum studies since then have shown no abnormalities . Examination today shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's current condition?
correctExplanation: Kernicterus occurs as a result of the deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in a newborn's brain, usually in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. It typically presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures. If untreated, it can cause long-term neurologic abnormalities, such as gaze palsies or sensorineural hearing loss. Unconjugated or indirect bilirubin is circulating insoluble bilirubin that is largely bound to albumin. It has not yet undergone conjugation in the liver. Causes of increased unconjugated bilirubin include hemolysis, breast milk jaundice, Crigler-Najjar syndrome, Gilbert syndrome, and physiologic jaundice. In newborns, causes also include maternal exposure to sulfonamide antibiotics, which displace bilirubin from albumin in the neonate, thereby increasing the free plasma concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin. Kernicterus typically occurs when the bilirubin concentration exceeds 25-30 mg/dL, which is commonly caused by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or Rh-hemolytic disease of the newborn, the latter of which was likely present in this patient given the discordant Rh status of him and his mother. Risk factors include prematurity, cephalohematoma or significant bruising, poor breastfeeding, and East Asian ethnicity. Treatment to prevent severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and subsequent kernicterus is phototherapy or exchange transfusion. Exchange transfusions are particularly useful in hyperbilirubinemia that is caused by anti-Rh(D) antibodies, as they allow removal of the antibodies as well as the bilirubin.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Avoidance of breast-feeding (Choice A) could be considered in breast milk jaundice or breastfeeding jaundice, although it is usually not required as the increased bilirubin concentrations seen are typically benign. Breast milk jaundice is hypothesized to occur because of the presence of beta-glucuronidase in breast milk, which deconjugates bilirubin and allows it to be reabsorbed. Breastfeeding jaundice occurs as a result of relative hypovolemia secondary to inadequate intake, which results in hyperbilirubinemia. Water supplementation (Choice B) is generally not advised in infants, as their kidneys are incapable of properly reabsorbing sodium, which results in hyponatremia. This can cause altered mental status and seizures. Water supplementation is not used to treat hyperbilirubinemia. Longer course of phototherapy (Choice C) could have decreased the overall amount of unconjugated bilirubin, as phototherapy converts indirect bilirubin into a water-soluble form that can be excreted. However, it would have been less effective in this patient with severe hyperbilirubinemia likely secondary to anti-Rh(D) antibody-mediated hemolysis. Antibiotic therapy (Choice D) is used in the treatment of neonatal infections, such as Escherichia coli or Streptococcus aga/actiae meningitis. Bacterial meningitis is associated with a high mortality if untreated, as well as prolonged neurologic complications, such as hearing loss, even when treated. A missed diagnosis of bacterial meningitis would have certainly led to neonatal demise or significant morbidity. Educational Objective: Kernicterus is caused by high concentrations of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, commonly in hemolysis because of Rh alloimmunization or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It is associated with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures as a result of deposition of bilirubin in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. If untreated, it can lead to long-term neurologic sequelae, such as hearing loss.

questionStem: A 4-year-old boy has had fatigue , decreased appetite , and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss over the past 2 months. He appears listless . His pulse is 80/min while supine and 105/min while standing , and his blood pressure is 85/60 mm Hg while supine and 75/45 mm Hg while standing . Serum glucose concentration is 465 mg/dl . Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones , 4+ glucose , and 1 to 2 WBC/hpf . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: A pediatric patient presenting with fatigue, decreased appetite, weight loss, and hyperglycemia raises suspicion for type 1 diabetes mellitus. Type 1 diabetes mellitus can also be complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and patients can present with DKA as their initial manifestation. DKA can also result from increased insulin requirements during times of physiologic stress (eg, infection) or insulin nonadherence. DKA occurs as a result of the accumulation of serum ketones such as beta-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs because of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Type 1 diabetes mellitus can also result in dehydration caused by hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and osmotic diuresis. This diuresis can result in dehydration, ketonuria, and orthostasis. Orthostatic vital signs are significant pulse increases greater than 20/min, systolic pressure decreases over 20 mm Hg, or diastolic pressure decreases over 10 mm Hg with changes in position from supine to seated to standing. Because of the patient's osmotic diuresis, orthostatic hypotension, and dehydration, the first step in care requires the administration of 0.9% saline intravenously for fluid resuscitation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Urine culture {Choice A) would not be the next appropriate step for this patient. Urinary tract infection is unlikely in a patient without symptoms of dysuria, urinary urgency, or frequency, and less than 5-10 WBC/hpf on urinalysis. Urinalysis discloses ketones and glucose, consistent with DKA, and the patient would benefit from fluid resuscitation. Oral glucose tolerance test {Choice B) is typically performed to evaluate for type 2 diabetes mellitus or for maternal gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks' gestation. Gestational diabetes can lead to an increased risk for congenital anomalies, spontaneous abortion and stillbirth, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. In a patient with a random glucose greater than 200 mg/dl and associated symptoms, the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus can be made. Measurement of hemoglobin A 1c {Choice C) is useful for the diagnosis and long-term management of diabetes mellitus. It would be less helpful in the acute management of a new diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and DKA. Administration of subcutaneous insulin {Choice D) can be helpful in this patient, although insulin should be administered intravenously for the management of DKA once the patient is appropriately resuscitated with intravenous fluid. In a patient with signs of dehydration and orthostasis, intravenous fluid resuscitation should be the first step in management. Educational Objective: Type 1 diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis can result in significant dehydration caused by hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and osmotic diuresis. The first step in care requires fluid resuscitation with intravenous isotonic fluids.
